items.title: VIEWPOINT: Auto policy’s tax paradox
items.description: Pakistan’s new auto policy was meant to take effect on July 1. It is yet to be finalised. Meanwhile, the automotive industry continues pricing vehicles, opening letters of credit, and signing dealer agreements in the dark — unaware of the tax burden those cars will carry next year. The latest bottleneck arose during the International Monetary Fund’s fourth review of the Extended Fund Facility. In late September, the Ministry of Industries and Production presented its draft Auto Policy 2026-31 to the IMF mission, but talks concluded without an agreement. The primary sticking point is the proposed one per cent sales tax on new energy vehicles. The Fund wants the standard 18pc rate. On a Rs10 million car, that single disagreement represents the difference between a tax of Rs100,000 and Rs1.8mn. Low tax rates matter, but the rate itself is only half the story. The crucial second half is defining what this policy is actually for. In FY26, Pakistan spent $16.9 billion on petroleum imports, a major portion of which was burnt on its roads. The government aims for 30pc of new vehicle sales to be electric by 2030, a transition estimated to save about $1bn annually in foreign exchange, 2bn litres of fuel, and 4.5mn tonnes of carbon emissions. For a nation recovering from devastating floods and choking on severe winter smog every year, these are not side benefits. They are the entire point. Low tax rates matter, but defining the policy is also crucial Both sides of the current argument are partly right. The Fund has watched Pakistan repeatedly carve up a narrow tax base through special rates and Statutory Regulatory Orders (SROs), knowing temporary concessions almost invariably become permanent. The ministry is equally right that electric vehicles cost more upfront, charging infrastructure remains thin, and buyers harbour deep anxieties about battery life and resale value. Imposing the standard tax rate overnight would reduce the 30pc EV target to a line on paper. However, the draft policy has a glaring weakness of its own. Customs duties on conventional cars are scheduled to fall sharply, but reports suggest this gap will simply be refilled through higher Federal Excise Duty and floor prices on imported vehicles – essentially building the same protective wall with different bricks. In the meanwhile, tax rates keep moving by notification. The concessional 8.5pc sales tax on most hybrids expired on June 30 with the expiry of the last auto industry development and export policy, causing taxes on locally made hybrids to jump to 25pc. Then, in September, the Federal Board of Revenue issued SRO 1525(I)/2026, bringing locally manufactured hybrids up to 2,000cc back down to 18pc. The relief was welcome, but the same car underwent three distinct tax rates in as many months, and the final adjustment came through SRO rather than any transparent policy. An investor deciding whether to establish an assembly plant does not mainly ask whether the tax is 1pc or 18pc. They ask what the tax will be in 2029, and whether that answer will survive the next budget cycle. A better structure would rest on five sensible pillars: First, agree on 18pc as the ultimate destination and legislate a clear roadmap to get there. Keep the 1pc tax rate until June 2027, when current concessions lapse, then step it up incrementally each year to reach the standard rate by FY2030. Low taxes in the early years build the market: China exempted electric cars from purchase tax for nearly a decade, and Norway waived VAT before both began phased rollbacks. Support should be generous at the start, but bound by a firm expiration date. Second, target the relief. A Rs30mn luxury import does not need the same fiscal cushion as a compact car, a taxi, or a rickshaw. Capping concessions by price or battery size concentrates public money where the public benefit actually lies. Third, set a clear tech ladder. The combined burden of duty and tax should be highest on conventional petrol cars, lower on hybrids, lower still on plug-in hybrids, and lowest on fully electric vehicles. Battery electric vehicles and range-extended EVs should share one tax structure at the bottom because their powertrain is fundamentally the same. Fourth, follow the National Tariff Policy honestly. Bring duties on fully built imports down as announced, eliminate additional and regulatory duties by FY30, and do not rebuild protectionism through excise duty. Maintain a moderate, transparent gap between duties on built-up imports and kits for local assembly, fixed for the life of the policy. Fifth, reward localisation through component tariffs, not sales tax exemptions. Offering low duties on battery packs, electric motors, and controllers for a fixed period from the start of local production is a far cleaner incentive that directly rewards genuine investment. The last important point is that established assemblers and vendor networks support over a million livelihoods, as per PAAPAM, and their fear of a uniform tariff cut is legitimate: localisation that took decades to build can be dismantled in a year. But ‘raw’ protectionism alone has failed to deliver scale or competitiveness. Local content in Pakistani passenger cars averages about 58pc, compared to roughly 80pc in India. The electric transition is a chance to rewrite that story. Localisation incentives should go to value added whether the carmaker is old or new, and vendors, who retool for electric components, should receive the same parts concessions and long-term financing. The government has a short window before the revised draft goes to the Cabinet. The right path forward is simple to state: agree on the end-state with the Fund, publish a binding dated schedule, target support where it moves the most people and goods, classify tax tiers by technology, and leave the rules alone long enough for someone to build a factory around them. Every day of delay is paid for in lost foreign exchange, dirtier air, and a target that slips further away. Low taxes will start the market. Only predictable taxes will build the industry behind it. The writer is an energy finance professional with over 20 years of experience. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, October 26th, 2026

items.title: Bobo-Dioulasso : la Police municipale sur le front des nuisances et de l’insalubrité
items.description: La Police municipale de Bobo-Dioulasso ne reste pas sourde aux plaintes des citoyens. Du 20 au 24 octobre 2026, à travers sa Direction de la Police de la Salubrité et de la Tranquillité Urbaine (DPSTU), elle a mené une série d'interventions dans plusieurs secteurs de la ville pour répondre aux préoccupations des populations. Les agents ont notamment traité des plaintes et remis des convocations au secteur n°04, rue Aguibou Traoré. Ils ont également constaté et géré des plaintes au secteur n°11, avant de se pencher sur les nuisances liées aux activités de saponification au secteur n°20. Les signalements des riverains portaient principalement sur l'insalubrité, les mauvaises odeurs et le déversement sauvage des eaux usées des ménages et des toilettes dans les caniveaux. Face à ces pratiques qui dégradent le cadre de vie, la Police municipale a rappelé les règles et engagé les procédures nécessaires. À travers ces actions, l'institution réaffirme son engagement à lutter contre toutes les formes de nuisances et à contribuer à l'amélioration du cadre de vie à Bobo-Dioulasso. Un travail de proximité qui montre que la salubrité est l'affaire de tous. items.title: Banks’ credit to manufacturers falls 26.8% to N5.19trn
items.description: *… as credit guarantees unlock N47bn *MAN seeks stronger guarantee coverage, N1trn stabilisation fund *Nigeria needs $35bn yearly to industrialise —BoI *Guarantees critical to boosting access to finance — CPPE *FG advocates coordinated financing framework By Yinka Kolawole Loans extended by Nigerian banks to the manufacturing sector fell by 26.8 per cent year-on-year to N5.19 trillion in the first half of 2026 (H1’26), from N7.09 trillion in the corresponding period of last year (H1’25). Read Also: Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate; 20 record capital gains This comes as manufacturers grappled with persistent financing constraints and rising operating costs. The decline also comes amid concerns over the availability of affordable, long-term funding for industrial production, with the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) calling for stronger credit guarantees and the full operationalisation of a N1 trillion Manufacturing Stabilisation Fund. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) Q2 2026 Statistical Bulletin also indicated a sustained decline as the outstanding bank credit to manufacturers declined by about 21 per cent between January and June 2026, from N6.57 trillion to N5.19 trillion. The 2026 monthly figures showed that credit fell from N6.57 trillion in January to N6.37 trillion in February, N5.77 trillion in March and N5.32 trillion in April. It declined further to N5.02 trillion in May before a slight recovery to N5.19 trillion in June. Despite the slight month-on-month recovery, the June figure remained substantially below the level recorded in the previous year. The contraction highlights the financing challenges confronting manufacturers amid high production costs, expensive electricity, logistics bottlenecks and exchange-rate pressures. However, the decline in outstanding credit does not, on its own, establish whether it resulted from reduced new lending, loan repayments or other changes in banks’ credit portfolios. Credit guarantees unlock N47bn Meanwhile, the National Credit Guarantee Company (NCGC) said it has unlocked N46.95 billion in loans for 67,512 borrowers across the country, renewing calls for credit guarantees to be expanded to improve access to finance for manufacturers and small businesses. Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of NCGC, Dr Bonaventure Okhaimo, said the credit was unlocked using N21.59 billion in guarantees to share lending risks with financial institutions. Nigeria needs $35bn yearly to industrialise — BoI The development comes as the Bank of Industry (BoI) estimates that Nigeria requires more than $35 billion annually to finance industrialisation and raise manufacturing’s contribution to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to 25 per cent. Highlighting the scale of the funding challenge, Managing Director of the Bank of Industry, BoI, Dr Olasupo Olusi, said no single development finance institution could close the gap. He stated: “It is a huge gap. BoI cannot do it alone from its balancesheet,\.” Olusi noted that the funding constraint was reflected in the bank’s 2025 pipeline, where loan applications reached N1.754 trillion against available funding of N645 billion, leaving a shortfall of about 63 per cent. He said the bank’s mobilisation of more than 2 billion euros through global syndication in 2024, which he described as the largest of such transaction by an African development finance institution, underscored the scale of capital required to support industrial expansion in the country. Unlocked credit commendable, but insufficient — MAN Reacting to the NCGC intervention, Director-General of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), Segun Ajayi-Kadir, described the credit guarantee model as an example of the risk-sharing mechanism manufacturers had consistently advocated. He said the amount was commendable but remained small relative to the estimated $35 billion annual industrial financing requirement. He stated: “Nigerian manufacturers are not unbankable, they are simply un-de-risked. “With MPR at 26.5 percent and CRR at 45 percent, banks would rather lend to oil and gas and government securities than to a factory in Kano or Port Harcourt or Lagos that is daily contending with power outage, logistics cost and high cost of forex. So we truly have a credit squeeze, not just high cost. “Now, this is where credit guarantees matter. A guarantee does not give money, but it gives confidence. Let us look at a situation where NCGC guarantees 60 percent of a facility. ‘’It tells the bank that if this manufacturer struggles because diesel jumps or production is disrupted one way or the other, someone will stand in the gap. That is how N21.59 billion could catalyse N46.95 billion – a multiplier of more than twofold. ‘’For our SMEs who form 70 percent of our membership and lack the 150 percent collateral banks demand, that is the difference between struggling and expansion, between 90-day overdraft and 5-year term loan to buy machinery to retool. “But let us be clear on scale. Nigeria needs $35 billion yearly to industrialise. That N46.95 billion was unlocked is commendable, within the context of the situation we are in. ‘’However, it is less than $30 million. It is a drop in that $35 billion ocean. So if we are to make any meaningful impact, we need to scale this model massively.” Ajayi-Kadir said MAN was seeking stronger guarantees and a dedicated financing facility to address the funding gap confronting manufacturers. “That is why MAN is asking for the full operationalisation of the N1 trillion Manufacturing Stabilisation Fund, to be domiciled with BoI, and for NCGC to be capitalised to provide 70 percent coverage for manufacturing at single-digit pricing. “Without that scale and without forcing transmission of MPR cuts to lending rates, guarantees will remain pilots. With scale, they can restore the N1.92 trillion we lost and finally align monetary policy with industrial reality.” Guarantees critical to boosting access to finance —CPPE Also commenting, Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE), Dr Muda Yusuf, described credit guarantees as critical to improving access to finance for manufacturing, agriculture and small and medium enterprises (SMEs). He said banks often perceived businesses in these sectors as high-risk borrowers, making guarantees necessary to reduce lending risks and expand credit allocation. His words: “Credit guarantee is very critical in enabling access to credit in the Nigerian economy. And one of the reasons the Nigerian banking system has been very reluctant in lending to some sectors is because of the risk of default in some of these sectors, particularly in the real sectors of the economy. And those businesses that are in the SME space. ‘’They are perceived as very risky. So in order to correct this or mitigate this challenge, credit guarantees have become extremely very important. “They have a very critical role to play in facilitating credits to the manufacturing sector to the agricultural sector and to small and middle enterprises. These sectors are perceived as very risky. “In order to facilitate credit to those sectors, we need this eh, ready guarantee uh skin. So it needs to be further strengthened. The capitalisation needs to be much more robust than what it is because you are talking of sectors that contribute over fifty percent of our GDP. And if you look at the credit allocation to these sectors, they are very, very low, compared to the potential they have in terms of contribution to economic growth and more particularly contribution to employment generation and contribution to food security and economic inclusion. “So, from a social and economic perspective, these sectors are very critical. But because of the risk inherent in investing in them, the banks have been, generally, very reluctant. So the credit guarantee scheme has a major role to play in mitigating the risk of lending to this sector. So the government needs to do a lot more to support this agency so that it can give a lot more support to this very critical sector.” FG seeks coordinated financing framework Meanwhile, Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has called for a coordinated financing framework involving government, regulators, development finance institutions and commercial capital providers. Speaking at a Ministerial Roundtable of the Industrial Revolution Work Group (IRWG), Oyedele said Nigeria must move beyond conventional bank lending by mobilising public balance sheets, blended finance, institutional capital, pension and insurance assets, as well as the capital market. According to him, the proposed National Industrial Finance Compact should ultimately be measured by whether manufacturers can access financing and deploy it to expand installed capacity, create jobs and increase export earnings. Oyedele also stressed that fiscal, monetary and industrial policies were interconnected, warning that an incentive, guarantee scheme or development fund that manufacturers could not effectively access was the same as having no policy. On his part, Minister of State for Industry, Senator John Enoh, said Nigeria’s financing architecture remained poorly suited to manufacturing because industrial investments required longer repayment periods than conventional short-term bank lending could provide. According to him, the challenge was not simply the availability of money but its cost, tenor and structure. “Our manufacturers do not lack ambition, they don’t lack orders, they don’t lack markets. What they continuously lack is the right kind of money,” Enoh said. He argued that investments in machinery, factories and production capacity required affordable, long-term financing, noting that businesses pursuing projects with gestation periods of 10 to 15 years could not reasonably be expected to repay loans within three or six months. “The issue is not that there is no money. It is the price of the money, the term of the money and the capital architecture into the factories,” he said. Enoh warned that the mismatch between financing structures and industrial investment needs could make trading more attractive than manufacturing, with implications for Nigeria’s industrialisation drive. He said the ultimate objective was to align capital with production. “Nigeria has entrepreneurs. Our job is to align capital with production, so we make more at home, employ more at home, and compete,” he said. items.title: Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
items.description: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile. “I am here. With you,” Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated attempts to re-enter the country failed. In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President Nicolás Maduro. The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, as leader, and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal that granted the US very favourable terms. Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands. She then began travelling to the capital, Caracas, in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters lined the route to the capital. She was photographed smiling as she leaned out of a car’s sunroof as she entered Caracas late Sunday night. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado greets supporters as she arrives in Caracas Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González, confirmed her arrival, writing in a statement: “I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil.” “Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!” González said. He added that he will soon join Machado in Venezuela to advance the country “toward freedom”. An advisor to Machado said in September that over the previous few weeks Machado had attempted to return to Venezuela seven times, but was denied each time. Reports say the US was involved in delaying her return, but it has denied it. It’s unclear what Machado plans to do next now that she’s back, but she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held . Her ability to return to her country has always depended on approval from the Trump administration, which it appears has now granted it. A staunch supporter of democracy, Machado won an independent presidential primary election – held outside the Maduro government’s official election authority – in 2023, earning more than 90% of the vote. Despite winning the primary, Maduro’s government barred Machado from running for office, accusing her of fraud and tax violations. Machado denied the allegations, calling them politically motivated. She spent her final days in the country hiding in safe houses before fleeing to Norway to accept the Nobel Prize. In the 2024 election, Machado’s ally González ran in her place against Maduro. The electoral authority, which is closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public. The opposition argued that González, not Maduro, won the election, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence. Maduro was removed from the country by US forces in January, and is currently jailed in New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges. He has pleaded not guilty. A spokesman for Machado called her return “a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future”. “We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the US Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support,” her spokesperson, David Smolansky, added. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said, “I don’t know anything about” her return, and added that he hoped she was “safe”. “I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe,” he said. In January, Machado visited the White House and gifted her Nobel Prize award to Trump . The committee that issues the prize had said: “It cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised his country’s role in securing her return through political reconciliation talks. “The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms Machado to Venezuela are the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks, which have already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed, and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile,” he posted on X. He added: “We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”

items.title: Brewing crisis of shrinking farm size
items.description: Pakistan’s agricultural crisis is generally framed around water scarcity, rising input costs, declining productivity and profitability and climate change. Yet another structural problem – the subdivision of agricultural land into smaller and scattered holdings – is worsening silently. Despite implications for farm efficiency, rural incomes and national poverty, the issue has received far less attention. The seventh Agricultural Census released in July has come up with figures that must ring alarm bells. The number of farms has increased from 8.26 million in 2010 to 11.10m in 2024 – a rise of 34.4 per cent. Over the same period, average farm size fell from 6.4 acres to 5.3 acres, a decline of 17.2pc. Even more significant is the number of fragmented farms, which rose from 2.83m in 2010 to 4.98m in 2024 – an increase of 2.15m, or more than 76pc. The average division of separate plots held by each fragmented farm increased from three in 2010 to seven in 2024 – an increase of more than 133pc. The general distribution of landholdings reinforces the picture. In 2024, 59pc farms were smaller than 2.5 acres, compared with 43.5pc in 2010. The proportion of farms below five acres rose from 64.7pc to 78pc, while more than 95pc are under 12.5 acres, up from 89.5pc in 2010. This skewed structure has implications for all; individual farms, sectoral performance and policy makers. For farms, smaller and increasingly dispersed holdings make mechanisation next to impossible, raise cultivation and supervision costs, limit access to credit and modern technologies, and reduce farmers’ capacity to generate marketable surpluses and cash for themselves. For many smallholders, farming is becoming less of a commercial enterprise than a means of meeting household subsistence needs At the sectoral level, it risks slowing productivity, weakening commercial agriculture and increasing rural poverty as families turn to off-farm employment to supplement their incomes. The policy implications are equally significant: improving agricultural performance requires more than addressing water scarcity and input costs. It demands initiatives to help smallholders overcome the disadvantages of scale, shared machinery services, equipment suited to small plots, accessible agricultural credit, cooperative farming arrangements, zoning and cluster development and incentivising voluntary land consolidation. For many smallholders, farming is consequently becoming less of a commercial enterprise than a means of meeting household subsistence needs. Muhammad Nadeem, a three-acre farmer from Okara, describes the transition: “When a plot falls below a certain size, subsistence farming and traditional rural practices – growing one’s own staple and fodder for livestock – take precedence.” Nadeem owns three buffaloes and divides his land between fodder, wheat and vegetables to meet his family’s basic needs. As the land is ancestral, he shares a return with his brother and sister. Farming is now a part-time activity: Nadeem and his brother work as labourers in Okara city, while his sister teaches at a local private school. “The land generates virtually no income because the yields are barely enough to meet our needs,” he says. It is also because of expensive fertilisers. Credit is another obstacle. Even local middlemen, who typically finance inputs, are reluctant to lend as they know the limitations of the family’s landholding. “For us, farming is no longer a viable source of income. We continue to cultivate only for it provides a staple for family and fodder for animals.” Nadeem’s experience shows how shrinking holdings can turn farming into a part-time survival activity, forcing families to seek off-farm employment while leaving no money for agricultural investment. The challenge becomes greater when land is divided into scattered, non-contiguous plots. Five consolidated acres at one location are very different from the same size spread across several parcels. Dispersed holdings increase the time and cost of land preparation, irrigation, crop protection and harvesting. They also complicate supervision, delay essential operations and make machinery less efficient to deploy. Former irrigation minister and south Punjab farmer, Mohsin Leghari, is deeply concerned about this trend. “Five acres in one place and five scattered across several locations are two completely different propositions. The latter increases cultivation costs, complicates mechanisation, makes supervision difficult, and delays critical farming operations,” he says. The shrinking average holdings could accelerate poverty and urban migration. Mechanisation presents a particular challenge with multiplying division of land. While machinery can reduce labour requirements, improve efficiency and help farmers complete time-sensitive operations, the high cost of purchase and maintenance is difficult to recover from smaller acreage, especially if scattered across different locations. Agricultural economist Mirza Irfan Baig argues that this problem extends beyond affordability. “For small farms, mechanisation is not simply a question of affordability or commercial viability; it is also a question of whether appropriate machinery is available in the first place,” he says. Baig explains that modern agricultural mechanisation largely evolved to serve large-scale farming, particularly in the West, where extensive, contiguous holdings allow machinery to operate efficiently across large areas. “Such machinery is not scale-neutral. Equipment designed for large, consolidated farms cannot be used efficiently on small, scattered plots. Its size, operating costs and capacity are not suited to smallholders. There is little incentive for manufacturers to develop specialised machinery for such a limited and fragmented market.” This creates a structural barrier to modernisation. Even if money is available, farmers may not find machines suited to their holdings. Buying large equipment individually is often uneconomical, while the lack of affordable, appropriately sized alternatives limits mechanisation and productivity. Addressing the problem does not necessarily mean the disappearance of small farms or the forced consolidation. Shared services, equipment rental markets, cooperative arrangements, zoning and clustering of land, and better coordination among farmers could help them acquire efficiencies of larger operations. Improved access to credit and technologies designed for small plots would also be essential. The policy makers now need to look beyond cultivated area and the immediate pressures of water scarcity, input costs and climate change, and deal with this structural issue. It is also necessary because subdivision of agricultural land is not merely a farming problem; it is also a question of rural livelihoods and national poverty. If millions of farmers struggle to earn a viable income from land, the consequences extend from rural dwellings to national poverty. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, October 26th, 2026

items.title: Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate; 20 record capital gains
items.description: By Peter Egwuatu Share prices of 55 companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) depreciated last week following profit taking by the investors. However, 20 stocks appreciated in price during the week under review. The week’s performance highlights the market correction facing the stock market as investors reassess their portfolios following the substantial gains recorded earlier in the year. Although selected stocks attracted buying interest, the recovery was not broad enough to offset losses in influential stocks, leaving the overall market sentiment negative. Analysts emphasised that the decline also came against the backdrop of rising international oil prices, which climbed sharply amid escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. While higher crude prices could support Nigeria’s export earnings and government revenue, their broader implications for domestic fuel costs, inflation and business expenses remain important considerations for investors. A review of the market performance last week showed that the NGX market capitalisation, which represents the total value of stocks, shed over N206 billion to close at N160.519 trillion from N160.725 trillion the previous week. In similar manner, the NGX All Share Index, ASI, close lower to 247,222.27 points from 247539.73 points. Meanwhile, a total turnover of 2.024 billion shares worth N110.773 billion in 173,113 deals was traded last week by investors on the floor of the Exchange, in contrast to a total of 1.659 billion shares valued at N98.088 billion that exchanged hands the previous week in 184,632 deals. The Financial Services Industry (measured by volume) led the activity chart with 1.111 billion shares valued at N53.908 billion traded in 81,787 deals: thus contributing 54.89% and 48.66% to the total equity turnover volume and value respectively. The Consumer Goods Industry followed with 394.039 million shares worth N9.811 billion in 17,912 deals. Third place was the Agriculture Industry, with a turnover of 147.170 million shares worth N2.821 billion in 7,462 deals. Analysing market performance and outlook, analysts at InvestData Consulting Limited, stated: “The near-term outlook for the Nigerian equities market remains cautious as investors balance the need to preserve gains against opportunities in selected stocks. The market’s substantial year-to-date appreciation provides important context for the recent weakness, as some participants may be reducing exposure after the strong returns accumulated earlier in the year. Continued selling pressure in banking, energy and other influential stocks could prolong the market’s consolidation. Further weakness in large capitalised stocks may continue to weigh on the benchmark even if selected equities record positive returns.” Vanguard News The post Stock market extend losses, 55 stocks depreciate; 20 record capital gains appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Gov’t bills face bipartisan scrutiny, not Parliament’s Finance Committee chairman’s orders – Adongo
items.description: Parliament’s Finance Committee Chairman, Isaac Adongo, says government bills undergo bipartisan scrutiny, with committee members shaping decisions rather than his personal instructions. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition, he said the chairman facilitates the committee’s work but cannot dictate its conclusions. “You don’t dictate to the committee what you want,” Mr Adongo said. His comments addressed concerns about whether he could challenge proposals from his own government, including those brought by his friend, Dr Ato Forson. Mr Adongo said the committee’s experience so far gave him no reason to be concerned. “Almost every bill that has come to us has been scrutinised on a bipartisan basis.” He pointed to the opposition members on the committee as evidence of the expertise involved in examining government proposals. They include the ranking member and former Finance Minister, Dr Amin Adam, whom he described as a “very critical and sharp mind”. He also named deputy ranking member Dr Stephen Amoah and Dr Gideon Boako. Mr Adongo said the committee’s responsibility extended beyond its chairman. He explained that its work must take account of the national interest. “Largely we agree on most of the things.” When disagreements arise, he said, they give members on both sides a chance to express their views on what should be done. He cited the bill establishing the Gold Board as an example. According to him, opposition members did not disagree with its principle but were uncomfortable with some provisions. Mr Adongo defended the decision to proceed with the legislation, pointing to what he called the “monumental impact of the gold board”. He nevertheless acknowledged that shortcomings could emerge and that the law could be revisited. “Of course, over time, there will be some lapses that can be identified, and a review is possible at any point in time.” Isaac Adongo expressed confidence that opposition members would support a future review if the executive returned to Parliament with proposals to amend clauses.

items.title: Ebola: FG identifies 53 contacts, offers N100,000 weekly support
items.description: *Says emergency support to cover feeding, accommodation, family upkeep *Patient improves as DG warns against delayed precautions *Rivers suspected case tests negative *Lagos steps up airport surveillance, says no suspected case *Zamfara activates Ebola surveillance after passenger arrives airport with 38°C fever By Chioma Obinna & Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja The federal government has identified 53 contacts linked to Nigeria’s confirmed Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, up from the initial 44, as health authorities intensify efforts to prevent further transmission of the virus. Read Also: Lagos govt on alert, says no Ebola case in state It also announced the approval of an emergency payment of N100,000 per person weekly for individuals placed in isolation or quarantine as part of efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak in the Federal Capital Territory, FCT. This came as Lagos State government weekend intensified Ebola surveillance at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport and strengthened public health preparedness, following the confirmation of an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja,. The Director-General of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, NCDC, Dr. Jide Idris, disclosed this at a briefing in Abuja yesterday. The government had initially announced 44 contacts, following the confirmation of the Ebola case in the FCT on October 20, 2026. Idris said the contacts, including healthcare workers, the patient’s spouse, domestic staff and other individuals who might have been exposed to the virus, had been identified, categorised and placed under monitoring. He explained that contact tracing was ongoing and that the number of contacts could change as investigations progressed and more information became available. The NCDC chief maintained that Nigeria had recorded only one confirmed Ebola case, while two additional suspected cases had been investigated. According to him, a suspected case in Rivers State tested negative, while investigations into another suspected case in the FCT were ongoing. He added that no contact had tested positive for the virus and that the FCT remained the only state with a confirmed case. “As of today, we have two suspected cases again. One in FCT, one in Rivers State. But we’ve tested the Rivers case; it’s negative. “So there’s no red line. We have that confirmed case, that’s the patient in the hospital. Contacts with symptoms, none. Contacts positive, none. States affected, only FCT now. Now, that’s the summary,” he said. The NCDC chief said the national incident management system had been activated at the highest level to coordinate the response, involving the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, FCT health authorities, other government agencies and technical partners. He stressed that being identified as a contact did not mean that an individual had contracted the virus, explaining that public health officials needed to monitor such individuals to detect any possible infection early. “Being identified as a contact does not mean that you have Ebola. It means that public health teams need to assess and monitor your health so that any possible infection can be identified early,” he said. He urged Nigerians contacted by public health officials to cooperate fully and provide accurate information about their movements, contacts and any symptoms they might have experienced. Samples collected On laboratory investigations, Idris said samples collected from the confirmed patient on three occasions had remained positive, while a sample taken from her husband tested negative. He added that genetic sequencing had been completed by two laboratory facilities to establish the genetic characteristics of the virus, with the findings being used to facilitate information-sharing with Ugandan health authorities. The NCDC chief said the agency had also strengthened the country’s laboratory capacity, with between nine and 12 public and private laboratories equipped to test for Ebola. He explained that testing for the confirmed case was being conducted at the National Reference Laboratory (NRL), adding that additional reagents and supplies had been positioned across the national laboratory network to improve preparedness. On clinical management, Idris said the confirmed patient was receiving treatment at an isolation facility, while arrangements had been made to accommodate additional cases if necessary. He disclosed that isolation and quarantine arrangements had also been established for contacts requiring closer monitoring. According to him, the agency was providing accommodation and feeding for contacts placed in isolation or quarantine, alongside temporary financial assistance to help them cater for their families during the monitoring period. He said the government had approved emergency payments of N100,000 per person weekly for contacts in isolation or quarantine. “Just to douse the tension, we decided we would do this. We provide N100,000 per person per week just to maintain their comfort and feeding because they were complaining,” he said. The NCDC chief further disclosed that the government had strengthened screening at the country’s international airports, with aviation authorities, immigration, customs and other relevant agencies working together to improve preparedness. He said passenger screening measures had also been expanded following the confirmation of the case, with health declaration forms required for passengers travelling into Nigeria from all countries. Idris called on public and private healthcare facilities to strengthen infection prevention and control measures, including patient screening, triage, hand hygiene, environmental cleaning, safe injection practices and proper medical waste management. He urged healthcare workers to maintain a high index of suspicion when attending to patients with symptoms consistent with Ebola, particularly those with relevant exposure histories. “Healthcare workers should not wait for laboratory confirmation before taking appropriate precautions. Protecting healthcare workers is essential to protecting the communities we serve,” he said.He also advised Nigerians to practise regular hand hygiene, avoid direct contact with the bodily fluids of suspected cases and promptly report possible exposure to public health authorities. If you have symptoms… According to him, anyone who develops symptoms following possible exposure should immediately contact public health officials and follow their instructions before visiting a healthcare facility. Idris assured Nigerians that the response would continue to be guided by evidence, with surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory testing and preparedness activities reviewed as new information became available. He urged the public to remain calm, cooperate with health officials and avoid spreading unverified information as the government intensifies efforts to prevent further transmission of the virus. Lagos steps up airport surveillance, says no suspected case Meanwhile, Lagos State government has intensified Ebola surveillance at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport and strengthened public health preparedness, following the confirmation of an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja. The government, which also assured residents that no suspected case had been reported in the state, urged them not to panic but remain vigilant, promptly report possible exposure and seek medical assessment if they developed symptoms, particularly after travelling from areas reporting Ebola transmission. The Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, disclosed this in a statement issued by the Lagos State Ministry of Health, saying the state was strengthening surveillance, risk communication and coordination with relevant agencies to ensure early detection and a rapid response to potential cases. According to the statement, the ministry, through its Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health, has conducted a strategic engagement and assessment at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport with airport management, Port Health Services and other aviation and public health stakeholders. The engagement focused on passenger screening, information sharing, infection prevention and control, and coordination of emergency response measures. The statement read: “Lagos State is ready to prevent, detect and respond to potential public health threats.” It added that the government was intensifying public enlightenment on Ebola symptoms, transmission and prevention, while urging residents to rely on verified information rather than rumours. “Ebola Virus Disease is a severe illness that can be fatal. It spreads primarily through direct contact with the blood and other body fluids of an infected person showing symptoms, contaminated materials, or the bodies of people who have died from the disease. Infection may also occur through contact with infected animals.” The ministry listed symptoms to watch for as fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Unexplained bleeding or bruising may occur in some cases. “Symptoms may develop between two and 21 days after exposure, the statement said, warning that early signs could resemble malaria and other common illnesses.” Abayomi advised residents who develop fever to undergo a malaria rapid diagnostic test before taking antimalarial medicines, in line with the state’s fever-management policy. Where the test is negative, a healthcare professional should assess other possible causes and determine appropriate treatment. The government also urged travellers arriving from areas reporting Ebola transmission to cooperate with Port Health Services, provide accurate travel and health information when requested, and comply with applicable public health guidance. “Anyone who develops symptoms during travel or after arrival should notify appropriate health personnel and seek guidance before visiting a healthcare facility. The statement advised anyone who suspects exposure, particularly following contact with a suspected or confirmed case, to contact public health authorities promptly before visiting a healthcare facility. Residents were urged to report suspected cases or relevant exposure concerns through the state’s emergency numbers, 112 or 767, or contact the Directorate of Epidemiology, Biosecurity and Global Health on 0802 316 9485. The government said it would continue to monitor developments, strengthen surveillance and response readiness, and provide verified updates as necessary. It stressed that early detection and prompt reporting were critical to preventing the spread of the disease. Zamfara passenger Zamfara activates Ebola surveillance after passenger arrives airport with 38°C fever Similarly, Zamfara State government has activated Ebola surveillance at Gusau airport and major motor parks after a passenger arriving from Saudi Arabia was found with a body temperature of 38 degrees celsius. The Commissioner for Health, Nafisa Maradun, disclosed this weekend while leading a medical team to flag off passenger screening at the airport. Maradun said the passenger, an indigene of Zamfara, was identified during screening and referred for further medical assessment. The state government has deployed medical personnel at the airport, motor parks and other entry points to screen travellers and support the early detection of suspected cases. Maradun said the surveillance measures were intended to prevent the virus from spreading to Zamfara, and urged residents to remain calm and cooperate with health officials. The state’s ministry of health also directed public and private health facilities, disease surveillance officers and local government health authorities to strengthen preparedness, improve screening and promptly report suspected cases. The government said it was working with relevant agencies, including the Nigeria Customs Service, NCS, and Nigeria Immigration Service, NIS, to strengthen surveillance at entry points. Transport workers are also expected to help identify and report passengers who may require medical assessment. items.title: FBR reforms, again?
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s warning against resistance to tax reforms has once again put a spotlight on the efforts to restructure the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR). The warning came after a pen-down strike call by the Inland Revenue Service Officers Association (IRSOA) in opposition to the reforms and subsequent punitive action against several officers. Since 2000, successive governments have borrowed hundreds of millions of dollars from the World Bank to restructure tax administration. However, persistent weaknesses in compliance, audit and enforcement raise a fundamental question: why have repeated reforms over two decades failed to deliver lasting results, and how will the latest transformation plan be different? The first major reform initiative began in 2000, followed by the World Bank’s approval of $102.9 million for the Tax Administration Reform Project in 2004. By 2012, the programme had established or upgraded 57 offices and facilities, including Large Taxpayer Units, Regional Tax Offices, Model Customs Collectorates and taxpayer facilitation centres. It also provided 11,445 items of equipment, including computers, alongside vehicles and improved office infrastructure. The reforms introduced partial automation, universal self-assessment and the transfer of sales tax and federal excise administration from Customs to Inland Revenue. However, manual procedures persisted, limiting efficiency gains. Much of the investment appeared to improve working conditions rather than revenue collection. The World Bank’s 2012 completion report recorded disbursements of approximately $48.4m and rated the project’s outcome as “moderately unsatisfactory”, warning of a high risk to its sustainability. Successive reforms since 2000 failed to produce results; investment in technology likely to remain ineffective sans central database to document transactions Former FBR chairman Shabbar Zaidi says he had over $200m available for reforms during his tenure but chose not to spend it on the projects unlikely to succeed without fundamental institutional changes. He says that investment in technology would remain ineffective unless the government establishes a central economic database to record and document transactions. Without reliable data on economic activity, tax officers could not effectively verify income declared in tax returns or identify concealed income, he argues. The priority, therefore, should be documenting economic transactions rather than spending more money on administrative reforms. Despite the earlier project’s un-favourable assessment, the World Bank approved another $400m under the Pakistan Raises Revenue Programme in 2019, followed by $70m in additional financing in 2025. Total approved financing for the two projects reached $572.9m, although this does not represent actual disbursements. A major institutional change came in 2009 with the creation of the Inland Revenue Service (IRS), integrating sales tax and federal excise with income tax administration. The restructuring triggered resistance from Customs officers and disputes over authority, senior positions and career progression. Both services subsequently expanded their organisational structures through dozens of new directorates and field formations. This expansion raises questions about whether new formations addressed operational needs or also accommodated promotions and postings. Their staffing, expenditure, overlapping responsibilities and contribution to revenue collection require independent evaluation. During the 2024 caretaker government, the then finance minister Shamshad Akhtar proposed separating Customs and Inland Revenue into distinct organisations with independent oversight. The proposals faced resistance from tax officials. Consequently, the restructuring was not implemented. International experience offers no single organisational model. India maintains separate central authorities for direct and indirect taxes, while Australia and Britain operate integrated revenue administrations. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) emphasise professional competence, accountability and effective enforcement. Tax expert Ikramul Haq says repeated restructuring and foreign financing would not improve FBR’s performance without fundamental institutional changes. “Technology is necessary. Faceless assessment, digital invoicing, production monitoring and intelligent risk selection can reduce discretion. They cannot substitute for institutional design.” He calls for separating tax policy from collection, merit based recruitment and promotions, and evaluating performance through voluntary compliance, recovery, refunds and reduced litigation rather than gross collection alone. He argues that corruption, poor performance and disagreement over reforms require separate treatment, while political accountability is equally necessary. The FBR’s revenue composition illustrates the continuing challenge. According to its FY25 yearbook, withholding taxes accounted for 58.2pc of gross direct tax collection, while collection on demand contributed only 4.6pc. These figures raise questions about the returns from investment in offices, vehicles, staff benefits and performance incentives. The Auditor General also identifies demand collection as an indicator of departmental performance. However, the biggest challenge is to minimise the tax gap in the sales tax, which is reported at over Rs3 trillion. Audit effectiveness remains another concern. The State Bank’s FY24 annual report noted that risk-based audits, introduced in 2019, had not been implemented across all functional levels. Manual interventions and poor recovery continued to weaken enforcement. The Auditor General’s FY25 report also identified deficiencies in tax assessments, recovery and litigation management. Procedural failures in tax litigation have attracted scrutiny. In December 2025, the Lahore Tax Bar Association sought an investigation into appeals dismissed by Lahore High Court because of missed statutory deadlines, raising questions about legal supervision and accountability within the revenue machinery. The government’s emphasis on rising income tax return filings also warrants examination. The FBR reported 6.7m returns by Oct 14, compared with nearly 5m during the corresponding period last year, an increase of 34.38pc. However, higher filing numbers alone do not establish improved compliance, particularly when differential withholding rates encourage taxpayers to enter the active taxpayer list. The latest FBR transformation plan focuses on digital enforcement. Faceless customs assessment began in December 2024, while the National Faceless Centre for Inland Revenue was established in Islamabad last month with nationwide expansion planned by June 2027. Automated case allocation and reduced interaction between taxpayers and officers may limit discretion and improve transparency. However, digital systems cannot independently guarantee competent audits, legally sustainable assessments or recovery of outstanding demands. The question is whether artificial intelligence, digital invoicing, production monitoring and automated risk assessment can improve tax compliance without stronger audit procedures and enforcement accountability. These technologies can detect discrepancies and verify transactions, but their effectiveness depends on proper investigation, legally sustainable assessments and actual recovery. For instance, identifying fraudulent input tax adjustments or mismatches between production and sales achieves little unless violations lead to enforcement action. The success of digital reforms should therefore be measured not by the number of suspicious cases detected but by recoveries, reduced fraudulent claims and measurable improvements in tax compliance. Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, October 26th, 2026

items.description: Présentée officiellement à Ouagadougou dans le cadre de l’Initiative Présidentielle pour la Relève et la Promotion de l'Élite Sportive (IP-RELIS) voulue par le Chef de l'État, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, la « Ligue de la Souveraineté » marque un tournant majeur dans la restructuration du football burkinabè. Portée par l'ancien international Adama Guira et soutenue par la ministre des Sports, Annick Lydie Djouma Pikbougoum/Zingué Ouattara, cette nouvelle compétition réunira 20 équipes réparties sur l'ensemble des 17 régions du pays dès janvier 2027. Alliant quotas de joueurs locaux, gouvernance transparente et création de 740 emplois directs, ce projet ambitieux vise à professionaliser la pratique sportive tout en renforçant l'inclusion sociale et l'ancrage territorial. Le paysage sportif burkinabè s'apprête à vivre une transformation d'envergure. Souhaitée par le Chef de l'État, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, la « Ligue de la Souveraineté » a été officiellement dévoilée à Ouagadougou par le Responsable Exécutif de l'Initiative Présidentielle pour la Relève et la Promotion de l'Élite Sportive (IP-RELIS), le Camarade Adama Guira. Lors de l'ouverture des échanges, la ministre des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l'Emploi, la Camarade Annick Lydie Djouma Pikbougoum/Zingué Ouattara, a souligné que cette compétition entend moderniser et restructurer le football national en y associant l'ensemble de la population et des acteurs du monde sportif. Cette réforme majeure vise à instaurer un cadre pérenne pour le développement du sport de haut niveau. Conçue comme un instrument de promotion de l'endogénéité sportive, la compétition impose un cadre organisationnel strict. Chaque club engagé disposera d'un effectif de 30 joueurs et de 7 encadreurs, permettant la création directe de 740 emplois dans le secteur sportif. Afin de valoriser prioritairement les talents locaux, la réglementation exige un quota minimum de 50 % de joueurs locaux parmi les titulaires, assorti d'une condition de résidence d'au moins six mois dans la zone du club. Sur le plan administratif, la Ligue s'engage à garantir une gouvernance transparente s'appuyant sur des mécanismes de contrôle indépendants conformes aux standards internationaux. La phase expérimentale de la Ligue de la Souveraineté se tiendra de janvier à juin 2027. Cette édition inaugurale rassemblera 20 formations représentatives des 17 régions du Burkina Faso, réparties en deux poules géographiques de dix clubs. La poule A, basée à Ouagadougou, regroupe les équipes Kadiogo 1, Kadiogo 2, Kadiogo 3, Oubri, Kuilsé, Liptako, Nakambé, Goulmou, Sirba et Tapoa. La poule B, établie à Bobo-Dioulasso, réunit Guiriko 1, Guiriko 2, Tannounyan, Nando, Bankui, Sourou, Djôrô, Yaadga, Soum et Nazinon. Ancien international burkinabè, Adama Guira a tenu à préciser le positionnement de ce nouveau rendez-vous sportif. La Ligue de la Souveraineté ne vient pas substituer le championnat national en cours, mais s'affirme comme une compétition complémentaire d'accompagnement. En offrant une vitrine d'exposition aux talents émergents de toutes les régions, ce projet entend accélérer la professionnalisation du sport et renforcer la cohésion nationale. L’article Initiative Présidentielle IP-RELIS : : 20 clubs issus des 17 régions prêts pour le coup d'envoi en janvier 2027 est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Death toll in Taraba bandits’ attack now 50
items.description: The death toll from an attack by gunmen in Taraba State has risen to at least 50, survivors and Amnesty International told AFP Sunday, after more bodies were discovered. Read Also: ‘We counted over 20 bodies after attackers left’ – Taraba massacre survivors Both police and Amnesty said some of the victims had drowned while trying to flee the attackers. Gunmen on motorcycles from a suspected “bandit” gang swarmed Binnari, in eastern Taraba, killing dozens of people shortly after Friday prayers. They also looted and burned stores. Taraba is sandwiched between northeastern Nigeria, which has a long-running jihadist insurgency, and the volatile central region, which faces criminal gangs known as bandits. Driven by money rather than ideology, the bandits in Nigeria target poorly policed rural areas, kidnapping for ransom and killing. “On Friday, we found seven bodies after the bandits attacked our community,” said Bashir Mamuda Musa, a resident of Binnari, in Taraba state. “The following day, Saturday, we discovered another 43 bodies in the river, bringing the total to 50,” he added. The new toll was confirmed by resident Abdullahi Zakari. “Many residents, including women and children, fled towards the river in an attempt to escape the gunmen,” Zakari told AFP. “Unfortunately, several people drowned while trying to flee the attack.” ‘Chased into river’ Bodies can often be difficult to recover when communities scatter. Some were discovered in a nearby river, according to both police and Amnesty. Police spokesman for the state Victor Msheliza told AFP on Sunday that they were still searching the area. Officers “found some (bodies) in the river” of people who were trying to escape, he said. Police were immediately deployed to the area after the attack, more deployments being sent, he said. Amnesty International gave a toll of 52 on Sunday, saying the attackers had come “in large numbers and set ablaze shops and market stalls”. “The bandits invaded in large numbers,… chased people and they headed toward the river to escape,” and drowned, Amnesty International Nigeria director Isa Sanusi told AFP. “Some were chased into the river by the gunmen”. Banditry has become a growing problem in northwest and central Nigeria, with powerful gangs battling overstretched police and military across hard-to-reach, rural locations. They raid villages and impose “taxes” on farmers and mining operations in areas with little state presence. Amnesty, in a post on X, blamed the Nigerian authorities for leaving some rural communities “at the mercy of gunmen that repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity. “Consistent failure of the authorities to bring the suspected perpetrators to justice is clearly emboldening impunity,” the rights group said on social media. items.title: Brazil's leftist President Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback
items.description: Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched a re-election victory , but his rival Flavio Bolsonaro refused to accept the loss and said he would seek to annul the vote. With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump. The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied projections to win an unprecedented fourth term. According to official results, he won 51.8 per cent of the votes to 48.2pc for Flavio Bolsonaro, with Lula pulling around 4.4 million more votes. The senator is the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country’s last election in 2022. Sunday’s vote was marked by confusion after a Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours as some polling stations had already closed. The move came at the request of Lula who complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting. Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as “unacceptable” and a “dirty trick”. “It is impossible to recognise the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections,” he said, stone-faced, in a brief speech in Brasilia. No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the country’s military dictatorship. “People went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country,” Lula said in his first comments after the win. Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula’s Workers’ Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate. Lula’s fight back After the first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies, declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro” and revamped their social media strategy. The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21pc to 19pc. Julio Canelo, 42, a lawyer celebrating in Rio de Janeiro hailed a victory for “the entire democratic spectrum.” “It was the result of the people mobilising, in the streets and online,” he told AFP . A fierce social media battle drew in Meta, parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, which Lula’s campaign accused of favouring his opponent with “algorithmic manipulation”. Meta denied this but acknowledged that some of Lula’s campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors. “We are going to have to regulate them,” Lula said of social media companies after his win. A bitter campaign marred by scandals and mudslinging laid bare the deep divisions that have plagued Brazil over the past decade. A country split in two Lula heads into a fourth term with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change. He rose from poverty to become president in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006. Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges were annulled on procedural grounds. In his third term, Lula oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters felt gloomy about the high cost of living and crime. Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, pitched himself as more moderate and jovial than his father and managed to galvanise conservatives as well as less ideological voters wanting something new. “We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro. Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030. He is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right. Lula’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump ’s United States. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard,” he said on Sunday. Lula received congratulations from Chile’s far-right president, Jose Antonio Kast, and Ecuador’s right-wing Daniel Noboa — both close Trump allies.

items.title: Northern Region NDC urges unity after internal polls, eyes 2028 victory
items.description: The Northern Regional Secretariat of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) has urged newly elected officers and unsuccessful candidates to close ranks after the party’s branch and constituency elections across the region. In a statement signed by Regional Secretary King Salam, the Secretariat congratulated the elected officers and urged them to lead with humility, fairness and a commitment to unity. “Your election is a clear expression of the confidence party members have placed in you. We urge you to lead with humility and fairness, and to serve as a unifying force for every member in your area,” the statement said. The Secretariat also commended unsuccessful candidates, saying their participation had contributed to the party’s democratic tradition. “The outcome of an election does not diminish your worth or your place in the NDC family,” it said. “The party still needs your experience, energy and commitment, and we count on you to remain active in its work.” The statement thanked delegates, supporters and party members for their peaceful participation, describing it as a demonstration of discipline and commitment to internal democracy. It urged members to put electoral differences behind them and focus on strengthening the party. “Competition was for a season; collaboration must now define our path forward. We call on all winners and losers, together with their supporters, to close ranks and build stronger bonds of unity,” the statement said. “There are no factions in the NDC. There is only one family with one goal.” The Secretariat said the priority was to consolidate the party’s gains, strengthen its structures and work towards victory in the 2028 general elections.

items.title: Kane primed to beat Yamal, Mbappe to Ballon d’Or glory
items.description: England captain Harry Kane is the favourite to win a wide open race to be crowned Ballon d’Or winner at a glitzy London ceremony on Monday, with Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe also in the running to be named the world’s best footballer. Read Also: 2026 Ballon d’or ceremony: date, time and how to watch The 70th edition of the award, established by the magazine France Football, will be hosted in England for the first time in recognition of the first winner Stanley Matthews and fittingly could have a first English winner for 25 years. Bayern Munich striker Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, leading the German giants to a league and cup double and England to the semi-finals of the World Cup. “I’d love to be able to achieve something like that. I would be a massive milestone in my career,” said the 33-year-old. But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and World Cup for Kane means the outcome is far from certain. “I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone,” he added. “I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know.” ‘I deserve it’ Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain’s Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d’Or winner one day. However, after a hamstring injury ended his club season early, he was far from the shining light of Spain’s World Cup triumph that was built on being the best collective unit. Yamal was pipped to both the player and young player of the tournament by his Barcelona team-mates Rodri and Pau Cubarsi. That has not diminished his bullish confidence ahead of the ceremony. “For me, Mbappe and me, we’re the two best players in the world,” Yamal said last month. “I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I’ve won.” Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France. The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies. His 10 World Cup goals made him the top goalscorer in the competition’s history on 22. “Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out,” said Mbappe. “Who am I voting for? Myself.” One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in FIFA’s rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist, allocating a maximum of 15 points down to one based on their ranking. The Ballon d’Or goes to the player who accrued the most points. Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player’s overall marketing value. Alexia Putellas is the frontrunner to win the women’s award for the third time with Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign to come to an end after an injury-hit year. Putellas, winner in 2021 and 2022, was part of the Barcelona side that regained the Champions League last season before moving to London City Lionesses. Her former club team-mate, Poland’s Ewa Pajor is the main challenger to Putellas after she netted 11 Champions League goals in Barca’s latest triumph. items.title: U/W Regional Chief Imam’s education fund supports 61 students with GH¢138,536
items.description: The Upper West Regional Chief Imam Educational Endowment Fund has disbursed GH¢138,536 to support 61 academically promising but financially disadvantaged students pursuing tertiary education nationwide. The support covers the 2026/27 academic year. The number of beneficiaries has risen from 44 in the previous academic year to 61, an increase of 38.64%. The Secretary to the Fund, Dr Saeed Moomin, announced the disbursement at a press conference at the forecourt of the Regional Chief Imam’s residence in Wa. He said the Chief Imam’s office continued to receive numerous requests for educational assistance, reflecting the financial difficulties facing families in the region. Established in October 2022, the fund selects beneficiaries through academic assessments, interviews to establish financial need and home verification visits. For some beneficiaries, the assistance has made the difference between continuing their education and putting it on hold. Ibrahim Salim, a Level 400 Political Science student at UBIDS, said financial difficulties had nearly forced him to defer his programme. “Due to this wonderful programme, wonderful foundation, I am able, let me say, in a few months to come, I will be calling myself a graduate,” he said. Amatus Ahmed, a Diploma in Business Studies student at UBIDS, said the initiative offered an important lifeline to young people from rural communities who struggle to secure financial assistance. Ayisha Yahaya, a Level 300 Basic Education student at Nusrat Jahan Ahmadiyya College of Education, also expressed gratitude for the continued support that had helped her progress through her studies. Stakeholders at the event urged beneficiaries to make good use of the assistance and contribute to the fund when they were able to do so. Former Wa Municipal Chief Executive, Tahiru Issahaku Moomin, called for unity in tackling poverty, describing it as a “common enemy” holding back the region’s development. “We have a bridge to cross, and that bridge… is the bridge to cross to success and prosperity,” he said. The Headmaster of Wa Senior High School, Adams Iddrisu Thirdman, cautioned students against diverting the money to other purposes. He encouraged them to excel academically and help sustain the initiative for future beneficiaries. The President of the Upper West Bar Association, Siddique Obeidu, commended the fund for investing in the region’s human capital. He said expanding educational opportunities for vulnerable young people could help reduce their risk of turning to armed robbery or drug abuse. Mr Obeidu added that the fund provided a dependable platform for citizens to support education and contribute to the region’s development.

items.title: Zelensky confirme qu'une réunion entre Russes, Ukrainiens et Américains aura lieu en novembre
items.description: Volodymyr Zelensky a confirmé dimanche qu'une réunion entre Russes et Ukrainiens aura lieu en novembre sous médiation américaine pour relancer des négociations de paix au point mort depuis le début de l'année. « Nous sommes prêts à discuter. S'il s'agit de la question territoriale, elle doit être abordée au niveau des dirigeants. Les autres questions relèvent des groupes techniques. Tout cela pourra donc être discuté en novembre », a déclaré le président ukrainien dans une interview à la télévision nationale. La Russie avait annoncé vendredi qu'une telle réunion était prévue en novembre à Abou Dhabi aux Émirats arabes unis, dans le cadre de récents efforts américains visant à réanimer les pourparlers de paix à l'arrêt depuis le début de la guerre israélo-américaine en Iran. Des négociations directes entre Russes et Ukrainiens avaient déjà eu lieu en 2025 sans aboutir à un règlement du conflit, les deux camps insistant sur leurs conditions. Dimanche, M. Zelensky a une nouvelle fois rejeté une série de demandes russes, estimant que les garanties de sécurité que réclame l'Ukraine à ses alliés occidentaux, la taille de son armée ou le choix de ses alliances « ne sont pas négociables ». Selon lui, la question des territoires que revendique Moscou en Ukraine « ne peut être abordée qu'au niveau des dirigeants », c'est-à-dire lors d'une rencontre entre Volodymyr Zelensky et Vladimir Poutine. Or, le Kremlin avait rejeté à plusieurs reprises une telle rencontre avant tout accord de paix définitif. Le président ukrainien a également une nouvelle fois appelé à un cessez-le-feu énergétique, alors que son pays redoute, comme en 2025, une douloureuse campagne de frappes russes cet hiver. La Russie rejette toute pause dans les combats avant un accord sur le fond, estimant qu'une trêve donnerait la possibilité à Kiev de se réarmer. items.title: Adongo defends GoldBod law’s passage despite opposition concerns, leaves door open to review
items.description: Parliament’s Finance Committee Chairman, Isaac Adongo, has defended the passage of the law establishing GoldBod despite opposition concerns about some provisions. He says the law can be reviewed if lapses emerge. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express Business Edition, he said opposition members did not reject the bill in principle. Their reservations concerned specific provisions. “The passage of the bill that led to the establishment of the gold board, for instance, from a political perspective, our colleagues do not disagree in principle, but their side of the divide was not comfortable with certain provisions,” he stated. He argued that Parliament needed to pass the law to allow the institution to begin its work. “Nevertheless, we needed to get that act out of the way, and you have seen the monumental impact of the gold board, so we needed to first get a handle on it.” Mr Adongo left the possibility of changes open. He acknowledged that implementation could expose weaknesses requiring parliamentary attention. “Of course, over time, there will be some lapses that can be identified, and a review is possible at any point in time.” He said he expected opposition members to support a review if the executive returned to Parliament seeking changes to clauses it believed could have been handled differently. He defended his position during a discussion about whether he could challenge government proposals, including those brought by Finance Minister Dr Ato Forson. Mr Adongo said the committee’s work involved scrutiny across party lines. He argued that its chairman could not impose decisions on members. “The reason is that almost every bill that has come to us has been scrutinised on a bipartisan basis.” He cited former Finance Minister and Ranking Member Dr Amin Adam, Deputy Ranking Member Dr Stephen Amoah, and Dr Gideon Boako as part of that scrutiny. Mr Adongo maintained that committee members had largely agreed on proposals brought before them. He said differences allowed both sides to express their views. For GoldBod, he said the passage was necessary despite the reservations, noting that any subsequent review would give Parliament another opportunity to examine provisions found wanting.
