items.title: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse, with five still missing
items.description: Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, as a search continues for five still missing. Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets on Friday. Dozens of builders were working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but they emerged largely unscathed. Those missing were believed to have been in shops at the building’s base. The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya. Police said on Saturday that they had launched a manhunt for the building’s owner and the contractor responsible for the site. The block collapsed on Friday afternoon while under construction, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors. Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had escaped unharmed, while the other had suffered non-life-threatening injuries. He had said on Friday that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped beneath the rubble. Police said the two survivors rescued on Saturday have been taken to hospital. Images from the scene in Nairobi’s Eastleigh area show the building’s concrete floors piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to reach those believed to be trapped underneath. Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations. Kenya’s National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether it had inspected the site before Friday. The National Police Service said it had launched an investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and determine whether anyone was criminally liable. It warned that anyone found responsible for negligence or violating building regulations would “face the full force of the law”. Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the building’s owners lacked the required paperwork to occupy it. He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise “developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards”. Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

items.title: Sécurité des systèmes d’information: un réseau national mis en place
items.description: Le ministère de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications électroniques a organisé la cérémonie de lancement du Réseau national des responsables de la sécurité des systèmes d’information (RSSI) et des points focaux cyber (REN-CYBER) des ministères et institutions, vendredi 23 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Le ministère de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications électro-niques renforce la sécurité des systèmes d’information au sein des administrations et des institutions publiques. A cet effet, il a mis en place le Réseau national des responsables de la sécurité des systèmes d’information (RSSI) et des points focaux cyber (REN-CYBER). La cérémonie de lancement a réuni des experts du domaine, vendredi 23 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Le secrétaire général du ministère chargé de la Transition digitale, Borlli Michel Jonas Somé, a rappelé que la sécurisation des systèmes d’information constitue désormais une exigence incontour-nable de la transformation numérique du Burkina Faso. Selon lui, la création de ce réseau vise à instaurer un cadre de concertation et de coordination pour renforcer la sécurité numérique des administrations et des institutions publiques. « La transformation digitale ne saurait se limiter à la dématérialisation des procédures et à la modernisation des services. Elle doit également s’accompagner d’une maîtrise accrue des risques, d’une protection efficace des actifs numériques et d’une préservation de la souveraineté numérique nationale », a-t-il déclaré. Pour le directeur général de l’Agence nationale de sécurité des systèmes d’information (ANSSI), Oumarou Sanou, le numérique joue un rôle croissant dans la productivité des services publics et la conduite des politiques de développement. Toutefois, cette évolution s’accompagne d’une augmentation des risques cyber, notamment la compromission des comptes, l’hameçonnage, les rançon-giciels et les fuites de données, a-t-il expliqué. Face à ces menaces, des dispositions techniques et réglementaires ont été prises pour protéger le cyber-espace, d’où la mise en place de ce réseau. Selon Oumarou Sanou, celui-ci vise à créer un cadre permanent de concertation, de partage d’informations et de renforcement mutuel des capacités entre les structures parapubliques, les acteurs privés et les organismes disposant d’infrastructures critiques. « Ces acteurs vont être le relais de l’ANSSI auprès des ministères et insti-tutions pour participer au renforcement de la sécurité des systèmes d’information dans ces structures », a-t-il précisé. Sécuriser les plateformes de l’administration Les membres du réseau auront notamment pour mission de contribuer à la sécurisation des plateformes numériques mises en place par l’administration avant leur mise à la disposition des usagers. « Dans ce processus de mise en exploitation, il y a des audits de sécurité et des recommandations qui sont faites. C’est le RSSI qui est chargé de suivre l’état de mise en œuvre de ces recommandations afin qu’on puisse sécuriser les plateformes et les mettre au service des usagers », a expliqué Oumarou Sanou. Il a souligné qu’il appartient à chaque responsable de promouvoir une culture de prévention, de veiller à l’application des consignes de sécurité dans les projets numériques et de soutenir la mise en œuvre des mesures collectives nécessaires. Le directeur général de l’ANSSI a également annoncé que des formations seront dispensées aux membres du réseau afin de renforcer leurs capacités. Pour le respon-sable de la sécurité des systèmes d’information de la Société nationale d’électricité du Burkina (SONABEL), Justin Mathias Meda Drabo, cette initiative constituera un cadre de collaboration et de partage d’expériences permettant aux membres de mieux sécu-riser les systèmes d’information de leurs organisations et d’anticiper les menaces. Mariama Claire MANDOMBA LOMPO

items.title: Justice, fairness, peace and Nigeria’s 2027 election
items.description: By ANTHONY OGBEIFUN As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election, the country stands again at a familiar crossroads: the choice between narrow, sectional calculation and the broader national demand for justice, fairness and peace. Elections are not merely contests for power. In a plural society such as Nigeria, they are also referendums on whether citizens believe the state belongs to all of them. Few Nigerian voices expressed this truth more memorably than the late elder statesman and Dan Masanin Kano, Alhaji Yusuf Maitama Sule. In May 2015, Sule led a delegation of the Northern Leaders Forum to congratulate then President-elect Muhammadu Buhari. His counsel on that occasion remains strikingly relevant today. Sule told Buhari: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” It was a simple statement, but one carrying the weight of Nigeria’s history. The country’s recurrent crises—ethnic suspicion, religious tension, electoral violence, insecurity, economic exclusion and the erosion of public trust—are not disconnected accidents. They are symptoms of a deeper disorder: the feeling among many citizens that fairness is selective, opportunity is unequal and power is used to reward loyalty rather than serve the common good. Sule understood this. “Behind every crisis anywhere in the world is injustice,” he said. And the antidote, he insisted, is “justice.” That insight should guide every political party, candidate, campaign organisation and voter ahead of 2027. A nation cannot be held together by slogans alone. Neither can it be governed successfully by force, intimidation or the temporary advantage of incumbency. Sule warned: “The world itself can never be governed by force, never by fear, even never by power. In the end, what governs is the mind. What conquers is the spirit and the weapons of governing the mind and conquering the spirit are justice and fair play.” Nigeria’s 2027 election will therefore test not only the popularity of candidates, but the moral seriousness of the political class. Justice, in the sense Sule meant it, is broader than court judgments or legal technicalities. It includes fair representation, equitable distribution of public resources, respect for the rule of law, protection of minorities, credible elections and equal treatment before public institutions. It means that a farmer in Zamfara, a trader in Onitsha, a teacher in Lagos, a fisherman in Bayelsa and a herder in Sokoto should all be able to expect the state to protect their lives, respect their rights and respond to their needs without discrimination. Sule put it plainly: “If you do justice to all and sundry — and I say all and sundry — because Allah says, ‘If you are going to judge between two people, do justice irrespective of the tribe, religion or even political inclination; justice must be done to whosoever deserves it.’” That standard is demanding. It rejects the politics of “our turn” when it becomes a cover for exclusion. It also rejects the politics of revenge, where one group’s victory is treated as another group’s defeat. Nigeria needs leaders who can rise above such thinking. The late Dan Masanin Kano was equally clear that justice must not be selective. “I am not asking you — and I know you will not — to discriminate against any part of Nigeria,” he told Buhari. “But I am asking you to do justice to all parts of Nigeria.” For political parties preparing for 2027, fairness must begin before the first ballot is cast. It must be visible in candidate selection, zoning arrangements, internal party democracy, campaign financing and the treatment of aspirants. When parties manipulate primaries, impose candidates, marginalise women and young people, or allow money to determine nomination, they weaken the legitimacy of the eventual winner. A flawed process produces a fragile mandate. And a fragile mandate makes governing harder, especially in a country where citizens are already sceptical of political promises. Fairness also requires issue-based campaigns. Nigeria’s problems are real: insecurity, unemployment, inflation, poor infrastructure, weak public services, climate pressure on agriculture and widespread poverty. These challenges do not respect ethnicity or religion. Candidates should therefore be judged on their plans to secure communities, create jobs, reform institutions, expand opportunities and restore public confidence. A campaign built on fear, sectional resentment or religious division may win attention, but it cannot build a nation. Sule’s warning remains urgent: force, fear and power cannot govern the mind or conquer the spirit. Only justice and fair play can. Sule linked justice directly to peace and development. “Justice will bring about peace,” he said. “Peace and stability are the pre-requisites of development.” No society develops sustainably in an atmosphere of fear. Investors hesitate where contracts are uncertain and violence is common. Farmers abandon land where insecurity prevails. Young people lose hope where merit is ignored and corruption rewards the connected. Communities retreat into distrust when they believe the state protects some citizens more than others. Peace is not merely the absence of gunfire. It is the presence of confidence: confidence that elections will count, that courts will be impartial, that public offices will serve the public, and that no region, faith or class will be permanently shut out of opportunity. The 2027 election offers Nigeria a chance to rebuild that confidence. But it will require more than campaign rhetoric. It will require electoral institutions that are visibly independent, security agencies that act professionally, political actors who accept results peacefully, and citizens who refuse to be used as instruments of violence. Nigeria does not lack talent, resources or ideas. What it often lacks is the disciplined commitment to justice that turns diversity into strength rather than division. Maitama Sule’s message was not addressed to one president alone. It was addressed to every Nigerian leader, in every generation, and to every citizen who hopes for a better country. As 2027 approaches, voters should ask hard questions: Which candidate will uphold the rule of law even when it is inconvenient? Which party will distribute opportunity fairly? Which leader will govern for all Nigerians, not merely for those who funded a campaign or share a regional identity? The answer should not be based on sentiment, ethnicity or fear. It should be based on justice. Sule’s counsel remains a compass: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” If Nigeria’s political class embraces that key, the 2027 election can become more than another contest for office. It can become a renewal of the national promise—a step towards a country at peace with itself, fair to all its people, and capable at last of fulfilling its vast potential. •Ogbeifun wrote in from Lagos. The post Justice, fairness, peace and Nigeria’s 2027 election appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ve Grand prix cycliste du Fonds Wassa Bondo: Soumaïla Ilboudo et Awa Bamogo, vainqueurs
items.description: Le sociétaire de l’AJCK, Soumaïla Ilboudo chez les hommes et celle de l’USFA, Awa Bamogo chez les dames ont remporté la Ve édition de la course cycliste organisée par le Fonds d’appui au sport et à la presse privée Wassa Bondo, le dimanche 25 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou. Deux millions de FCFA et un million de FCFA. Ce sont les gains en espèces des deux grands vainqueurs du Ve grand prix cycliste du Fonds Wassa Bondo. Le dimanche 25 octobre la lutte pour monter sur la plus haute marche du podium a été âpre entre les 193 coureurs. Lâchés au contournement route de Saponé à 8h passées, Bur-kinabè, Maliens et Nigériens ont vite imprimé un rythme exceptionnel à la course. En témoigne la vitesse moyenne horaire finale mesurée à 44,191km/h. Après 2h46’03’’, c’est Soumaïla Ilboudo qui, suite au verdict de la photofinish franchit en premier la ligne d’arrivée. Il devance au sprint groupé, les coureurs de l’AS BESSEL Souleymane Koné (2e) et Mohamadi Ilboudo (3e). Ces derniers empochent respectivement un million et 500000 F CFA. Au programme, 122,300 km étaient à couvrir avec un circuit fermé de 5,500km à boucler 11 fois devant plusieurs autorités et un public mobilisé en grand nombre pour la circonstance sur le boulevard Thomas-Sankara. Après 30 km de route, Idrissa Ouangrawa de l’USFA enlève le premier point chaud devant Daouda Soulama de l’AJCK et Barthélémy Yaméogo de l’USFA. Le second point chaud disputé à Nioko2 sur la route nationale 3 a été remporté par Harouna Ilboudo au km 54,51. Au premier tour du circuit sur le boulevard, ce sont Alassane Ouattara de MAKAFA et Vincent Mouni de BESSEL qui ont réussi à creuser un écart d’une dizaine de secondes sur le peloton qui se partagent les deux premières récompenses de la 1re prime. Alassane Ouattara va s’adjuger également la prime suivante sur la ligne après 78,60 km parcourus devant Ousmane Kabré et Souleymane Koné de BESSEL. Il est devancé pour la 3e prime par Ousmane Kabré mais revient à la charge pour s’imposer devant ce dernier pour la dernière après 103,40 km. A 33 km de l’arrivée, le peloton s’est de nouveau regroupé. Objectif atteint La tentative d’échappée d’une dizaine de cyclistes qui a prospéré jusqu’à 24 secondes d’écart a été annihilée après un tour de piste. L’on compte désormais à cette étape de la course, 50 abandons à l’issue de plus de deux heures de compétition à une vitesse de plus de 44k/h. Ils ne seront plus que 34 sur les 93 au départ au moment d’aborder le dernier tour et ne se lâcheront plus les roues jusqu’au sprint final. Un peu plus tôt, les dames se sont mesurées sur le circuit fermé d’une distance totale de 40,800 km. L’ambassadrice du club militaire, l’USFA, Awa Bamogo talonnée par sa rivale légendaire Lamoussa Zoungrana de l’AS BESSEL a remporté la compétition chez les dames. Temps mis : 1h6’00’’ soit une vitesse de 37,090 k/h. Elle est récompensée d’une enveloppe d’un million de FCFA. Lamoussa Zoungrana reçoit 750 000 FCFA et sa coéquipière Latifat Sawadogo (3e), 500000 FCFA. La directrice générale du Fonds Wassa Bondo, Ida Ouédraogo, a rappelé que cette compétition s’inscrivait dans la dynamique de préparation des Etalons pour le 37e tour du Faso. Et au regard des perfor-mances enregistrées, l’initiative a atteint son objectif selon les techniciens et les autorités présentes parmi lesquelles la mi-nistre chargée des Sports. « Nous avons vu des équipes qui se sont bien battues. Nous étions hier sur un autre site où la vitesse était à 43km/h, aujourd’hui nous sommes à plus de 44km/h, ce sont des performances qui indi-quent que notre équipe nationale s’est bien préparée », s’est réjouie Annick Pickbougoum. Les équipes invitées du Mali et du Niger ont reçu des prix spéciaux d’une valeur de 500000 F CFA chacune. La meilleure équipe de cette édition est AS BESSEL. Voro KORAHIRE

items.title: Making gas operations safer
items.description: Nigeria’s ambition to expand the use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) must be matched by a serious commitment to safety. The Nigerian Association of Liquefied Petroleum Gas Marketers (NALPGAM), at its recent webinar on operational excellence and compliance, warned that rising consumption alone cannot guarantee a sustainable industry. Every facility must be safe, every operator competent, every process compliant and every customer protected. The warning is timely. LPG offers households and businesses a cleaner alternative to firewood, charcoal and other polluting fuels, but it is highly flammable. Leaking gas, overfilled cylinders, defective valves, poorly maintained equipment and unsafe storage can turn premises into disaster scenes. Illegal decanting and unauthorised propane blending compound these risks, endangering workers, consumers and neighbouring communities. Such practices must not be treated as commercial shortcuts. NALPGAM’s proposed Standard of Operational Excellence, built around safe facilities, trained personnel, compliant processes and consumer protection, deserves support. But a declaration is not enforcement. The association must translate its aspiration into measurable obligations for members, while the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) must sustain inspections, investigate violations and apply sanctions. Operators should maintain equipment, verify cylinder integrity, provide fire and gas-detection systems, and report incidents promptly. Regulators should publish inspection and enforcement data so the public can judge progress. Technology can strengthen this effort. Smart filling systems, calibrated load cells, flow meters, automated tank gauges and vehicle tracking can improve measurement, trace product movements and expose losses or suspicious transactions. Digital tools, however, are no substitute for trained staff, independent checks and functioning emergency procedures. Small operators may need affordable training, technical guidance and finance for compliant upgrades; such assistance must never become an excuse to relax minimum safety standards. Safety also has an economic dimension. Accidents destroy lives, property, investment and public confidence. Consumers who fear explosions or suspect short-changing may avoid cooking gas, frustrating efforts to broaden its use. Reliable cylinder traceability, approved exchange arrangements, accurate measurement and clear consumer information can build trust. Government should involve marketers in LPG penetration and cylinder recirculation programmes, while improving supply and distribution infrastructure to make fuel more accessible and affordable. The stakes extend beyond individual kitchens. Wider adoption of LPG can reduce household exposure to smoke from solid fuels and ease pressure on forests. A safer, better-regulated market can also attract investment, support certified local cylinder manufacturing, create jobs and deepen Nigeria’s energy economy. The national target of five million tonnes of annual LPG consumption by 2030 will mean little if expansion outpaces safety capacity. Government, regulators and marketers must turn promises into deadlines, audits, transparent reporting and consequences for negligence. Safety must govern every delivery, filling and transaction. Only then can Nigerians embrace gas with confidence, the environment benefit, and the industry become a pillar of economic diversification. items.title: When a police officer is caught at crime scene
items.description: By Owolola Adebola The sight of a police officer at a crime scene should ordinarily inspire confidence, reassurance and hope. It should signal the arrival of law, the protection of innocent citizens and the beginning of justice for victims. But what happens when the very officer expected to prevent a crime is caught participating in it? What happens when the uniform that should represent honour becomes a disguise for criminality? At that moment, the incident transcends the conduct of an individual officer. It becomes a test of the integrity of the police institution, the effectiveness of internal supervision and the willingness of the state to hold its own agents accountable. A police officer caught at a crime scene under suspicious circumstances presents a troubling contradiction. The law enforcement agent who should be chasing criminals may suddenly find himself on the other side of the law. The individual entrusted with protecting lives and property may become a threat to the very people whose safety he has sworn to defend. Such an incident demands serious investigation, not institutional excuses. Of course, insanity creeps in when the uniform becomes a shield for criminality because the police uniform carries authority. It commands attention, opens doors and gives its wearer powers that ordinary citizens do not possess. These privileges are granted for public service, not personal enrichment, intimidation or criminal enterprise. Unfortunately, when an officer abuses that authority, the consequences can be devastating. A police officer involved in robbery, kidnapping, extortion, unlawful possession of weapons or the protection of criminal gangs does more than violate the law. He exploits public confidence and undermines the institution he represents. The situation becomes even more disturbing when an officer is found at a scene where criminal activities are taking place and credible evidence suggests that he may be involved. Rather than automatically treating the officer as guilty, the authorities must establish what brought him there, what role he played and whether his presence was lawful. An officer could be at a crime scene to prevent an offence, rescue a victim, investigate an incident or arrest suspects. But where evidence points to complicity, the uniform must offer no protection from investigation. The badge is not a licence to commit crime. It is a badge of honour and not a badge of horror. The uniform is not immunity from prosecution. And membership of the police force must never become a passport to escape justice. Public cooperation is indispensable to effective policing. Citizens provide information, identify suspects, report suspicious activities and assist investigations because they expect the police to act in their interest. But when officers themselves become suspects in criminal investigations, that confidence suffers. A trader who sees a police officer allegedly collaborating with armed robbers may hesitate before reporting the next suspicious movement. A family whose relative has been victimised by an officer may lose faith in the complaint process. A community that repeatedly encounters alleged police misconduct may begin to regard law enforcement as a source of danger rather than protection. This erosion of trust gives criminals additional room to operate. Witnesses become reluctant to speak, victims withdraw complaints and valuable intelligence disappears into a climate of suspicion. The damage is not limited to the immediate victims. Honest police officers also pay the price. Their sacrifices, courage and commitment can be overshadowed by the misconduct of colleagues who betray the institution. It is therefore in the interest of the police themselves to confront criminality within their ranks decisively. Protecting a compromised officer does not protect the institution; it places the reputation of the entire force at risk. In a way, investigation must replace cover-up. Whenever a police officer is apprehended at a crime scene under circumstances suggesting criminal involvement, the first responsibility of the authorities is to establish the facts. The scene must be secured. Weapons, documents, surveillance footage and other relevant evidence must be preserved. Witnesses should be interviewed without intimidation, and the officer’s movements and communications should be examined where legally authorised. Where there is credible evidence of wrongdoing, the officer should be subjected to the same lawful investigative process applicable to other suspects. Rank, seniority, political connections and years of service must not determine whether an investigation proceeds. At the same time, fairness requires that allegations be distinguished from proven facts. Being present at a crime scene does not, by itself, establish guilt. The officer must have an opportunity to respond to the allegations, and the investigation must respect due process. This balance is essential. Accountability without fairness can become persecution, while fairness without accountability can become an excuse for impunity. The Nigeria Police Force must demonstrate that its disciplinary procedures are effective and that credible allegations of criminal conduct receive prompt, impartial attention. Where the evidence establishes criminal responsibility, administrative discipline alone may be insufficient; criminal prosecution should follow where warranted. A transfer to another command, quiet retirement or internal reprimand must not become a convenient substitute for justice in a serious criminal case. Come to Think of It: The Responsibility of Police Leadership Police leadership has a duty to ensure that officers understand the limits of their authority and the consequences of abusing it. Recruitment, training, supervision and disciplinary systems must reinforce the principle that integrity is as important as operational competence. Commanders must also be prepared to investigate officers under their supervision without fear or favour. Where a superior officer obstructs an investigation, destroys evidence or shields a colleague from accountability, that conduct must itself attract scrutiny. Independent oversight, accessible complaint channels and protection for whistle-blowers can help citizens report misconduct without fear of retaliation. Regular audits of police operations, transparent reporting of disciplinary outcomes and effective collaboration with relevant oversight bodies can further strengthen accountability. In addition, technology also has a role to play. Properly managed body cameras, vehicle tracking systems, digital duty records and evidence-management procedures can help establish where officers were deployed and what occurred during an operation. Such tools must be governed by clear rules to protect privacy, preserve evidence and prevent manipulation. The objective is not to portray every police officer as a potential criminal. It is to build a system in which honest officers are protected, misconduct is detected and those who abuse their authority cannot easily escape scrutiny. Justice Must Be Seen to Be Done When a police officer is caught at a crime scene and credible evidence indicates possible criminal involvement, the public deserves more than official silence. It deserves a credible investigation and, where necessary, prosecution. The authorities must communicate verified developments responsibly without compromising investigations or prejudicing a fair trial. If the officer is cleared, that outcome should also be acknowledged. Justice must not be manipulated to satisfy public anger, political interests or institutional embarrassment. Ultimately, the true strength of a police force is not measured by the number of arrests it makes, the weapons it recovers or the criminals it parades before television cameras. Its strength is measured by its willingness to obey the law it enforces. A police officer who catches a criminal deserves commendation. An officer who becomes involved in crime must face the consequences established by law. There should be no confusion between the two. Nigeria cannot build a society governed by law if those entrusted with enforcing that law are permitted to stand above it. The police uniform must remain a symbol of service, discipline and courage—not a hiding place for criminal conduct. When an officer is caught at a crime scene, the decisive question is not whether the institution can protect its reputation by remaining silent. It is whether the institution possesses the courage to protect that reputation by telling the truth, investigating the evidence and allowing justice to take its course. The uniform may command respect, but only integrity can sustain it. And when the hand entrusted with enforcing the law is suspected of breaking it, the law must be allowed to do its work without fear, favour or compromise. •Adebola, the State Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Ondo State Chapter, wrote in from Akure. The post When a police officer is caught at crime scene appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
items.description: Gabon says it has lifted a social media ban imposed eight months ago, a move that drew widespread criticism at the time. The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country’s media regulator for comment. The HAC introduced the ban on 17 February, saying online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country. The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure. Many turned to VPNs to keep accessing social media sites after the ban. The ban came at a time when Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election. Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions. The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power. Nguema won last year’s elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup ended more than five decades of Bongo family rule. At the time, he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information.

items.title: Fourniture locale dans les mines: les achats en forte progression
items.description: Le Secrétariat permanent du contenu local et de la promotion des investissements a organisé, du 20 au 22 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou, des rencontres sectorielles sur la fourniture de biens et services aux sociétés minières. Le contenu local gagne du terrain dans le secteur minier burkinabè. De 33 % en 2022, la part des achats locaux de biens et services des sociétés minières est passée à 57,84 % en 2025, selon les données présentées par l’administration des mines. Pour consolider cette dynamique, les acteurs du secteur se sont retrouvés à Ouagadougou, du 20 au 22 octobre 2026, pour échanger autour du fret et du transit, de la location d’engins miniers et des pièces de rechange, ainsi que des Equipements de protection individuelle (EPI). Organisées par le Secrétariat permanent du contenu local et de la promotion des investissements, en collaboration avec la Chambre des mines du Burkina (CMB), la Chambre de commerce et d’industrie du Burkina Faso (CCI-BF) et l’Alliance des fournisseurs burkinabè de biens et services miniers (ABSM), ces rencontres visent à identifier des solutions pour renforcer la participation des entreprises nationales aux approvisionnements miniers. Pour le secrétaire permanent, Zoéwendtaalé Zéphirin Zongo, ces échanges permettent aux fournisseurs, aux sociétés minières et à l’administration de confronter leurs difficultés et de rechercher des réponses concertées. « Nous attendons des recommandations fortes et opérationnelles pour améliorer la fourniture de biens et de services », a-t-il indiqué. Il a également relevé l’importance de prendre en compte les changements intervenus dans l’organisation du fret et du transit, notamment avec Faso Transit Logistique, ainsi que le rôle de l’Office national de sécurisation des sites miniers (ONASIM). La qualité et le financement en question La cheffe de service par intérim de la promotion de la chaîne de valeurs minières, Germaine Ki Lingani, a souligné les avancées enregistrées depuis l’adoption de la loi n°017-2024/ALT du 18 juillet 2024 relative au contenu local dans le secteur minier. Elle a notamment rappelé les mécanismes de préférence nationale, les obligations de fourniture locale et les dispositions encadrant la sous-traitance et la cotraitance. Les besoins d’approvisionnement prévisionnels des sociétés minières pour 2026 dépassaient 2 000 milliards F CFA, dont plus de 267 milliards F CFA. Pour les équipements de protection individuelle, les achats sont passés de plus de 4 milliards F CFA en 2023 à plus de 10 milliards en 2025. Malgré ces opportunités, plusieurs obstacles freinent les fournisseurs nationaux. Germaine Ki Lingani a notamment cité l’accès difficile au financement, l’insuffisance de la production locale de certains biens et les tentatives de contournement de la réglementation. Elle a aussi insisté sur la nécessité d’améliorer la compétitivité des entreprises, les normes de qualité et les relations entre fournisseurs et sociétés minières. Le représentant de la CMB, Ezidor Bazemo, a, pour sa part, insisté sur le professionnalisme. Selon lui, la fourniture aux mines exige une bonne connaissance des produits, de leurs caractéristiques et des exigences techniques. Il a également plaidé pour la mutualisation des moyens afin de renforcer leurs capacités d’intervention. Pour le représentant de Burkina Mining Company, Bouama Arnaud Wali, les rencontres constituent un cadre pour examiner les difficultés d’approvisionnement et identifier les possibilités offertes aux entreprises locales. Il a particulièrement insisté sur la conformité des équipements de protection individuelle aux normes de sécurité. « Par exemple, si le cyanure n’est pas de qualité, cela peut avoir des conséquences sur la santé de l’employé qui fait la manutention », a-t-il averti. Adama SAWADOGO

items.title: Lula réélu président du Brésil pour un quatrième mandat
items.description: Le président brésilien de gauche Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a été réélu dimanche, obtenant à presque 81 ans un quatrième mandat inédit à la tête du plus grand pays d'Amérique latine. Le Brésil n'a finalement pas viré à droite comme l'Argentine, le Chili ou encore la Colombie, tous soutenus par le président américain Donald Trump. Il reste l'un des rares bastions progressistes en Amérique latine. Avec 51,76 % des voix contre 48,24 % pour le sénateur conservateur Flavio Bolsonaro après un dépouillement quasi complet, le vétéran a déjoué tous les pronostics. Il avait été devancé au premier tour par le fils de l'ancien président d'extrême droite Jair Bolsonaro (2019-2022). « Je suis très émue. C’est une victoire historique pour le président Lula. Le peuple s'est mobilisé, s'est uni » , dit à l'AFP Mariana Andrade, avocate de 33 ans, qui a suivi le dépouillement sur un écran géant dans le centre-ville de Rio de Janeiro. Lors de ce quatrième mandat, la marge de manoeuvre du chef de l'Etat s'annonce cependant limitée après le raz-de-marée conservateur aux législatives il y a trois semaines. La campagne a montré combien le pays reste divisé et une controverse a même perturbé la journée électorale. Sur décision d'un juge de la Cour suprême, le vote a été prolongé de deux heures, après un recours de l'équipe de campagne de Lula. Dénonçant « une chose abominable » , le président sortant a affirmé que des électeurs ont été « empêchés de voter » . Selon lui, des bus ont été retirés de la circulation dans des villes comme Sao Paulo (sud-est), dirigée par un maire de droite, ou Salvador de Bahia, dans son fief du Nord-Est. Mesures sociales Du point de vue personnel, la réélection de Lula est le couronnement d'une trajectoire hors du commun. Et un ultime pied de nez au destin pour l'ancien gamin pauvre du Pernambouc (nord-est). Il détenait déjà un record: aucun président démocratiquement élu n'a dirigé aussi longtemps le Brésil. Celui qui est déjà un des dirigeants les plus âgés au monde aura 85 ans au terme de son nouveau mandat en 2030. Il totalisera ainsi 16 années au pouvoir, après un premier passage à la présidence de 2003 à 2010. Vétéran inoxydable à l'heure du dégagisme, Lula a conjuré l'usure du temps et une lassitude très forte à l'égard de son Parti des travailleurs (PT). Le PT reste associé par beaucoup aux scandales qui l'ont abîmé dans les années 2000. Son leader lui-même a connu l'opprobre d'une condamnation pour corruption qui lui a valu 580 jours en prison en 2018-2019, avant d'être annulée pour motifs de procédure. Pour renverser le score, l'icône internationale de la gauche a multiplié dans la dernière ligne droite les mesures populaires et souvent coûteuses. Le premier président brésilien issu de la classe ouvrière a notamment revalorisé la Bolsa Familia, son programme social phare destiné aux familles les plus pauvres. Défense du drapeau Durant sa campagne, Lula a brandi l'étendard de la souveraineté, face aux pressions commerciales et diplomatiques des Etats-Unis. Les électeurs doivent « choisir un pays où le drapeau est respecté » , a-t-il dit d'une voix fatiguée après avoir voté, accusant son rival de vouloir « gouverner avec le drapeau américain ». Donald Trump s'est toutefois gardé d'apporter un soutien explicite au fils Bolsonaro. Interrogé dimanche au sujet du scrutin, le président américain s'est contenté de dire: « On observe ». Mais c'est Meta qui dans les derniers jours a été la cible des attaques de la gauche. La maison mère de Facebook, WhatsApp et Instagram a été accusée par l'équipe de Lula d' »ingérence » et de favoriser Flavio Bolsonaro sur ses plateformes. Le géant américain de la tech a nié tout parti pris, mais reconnu des « problèmes techniques » ayant pénalisé la campagne de la gauche sur ses plateformes. The post Lula réélu président du Brésil pour un quatrième mandat appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: We never left Egypt, only prodigals need to return home, by Owei Lakemfa
items.description: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu told Nigerians on October 19, 2026, that they will not return to Egypt. He seems unaware that Egypt is our ancestral home and that we never left and will never leave. This Niger Area is the land of milk and honey we inherited from our fathers and mothers. We were never slaves in this land, will fight any attempt to enslave us; therefore, we never had any reason to flee. We never had any reason to part ways with the sea or for the sea to part ways for us. We never needed to wander in any desert for forty years or more, seeking pathways to freedom or prosperity. This has never been, and will never be, our portion in life. Ancient Egypt is the origin of modern civilisation. It civilised the Greeks and Romans, who were its pupils before they passed that civilisation to the rest of Europe. The peoples who make up Nigeria were self-sufficient, with viable city-states and empires, and well-schooled in their non-Western education. One of the natural endowments of this beautiful country is oil. We began producing it in commercial quantities from 1956–57. We were self-sufficient in it, including local refining, with the country running four refineries. As then Head of State Yakubu Gowon said in 1973: “Money is not Nigeria’s problem, but how to spend it.” What has happened to Nigeria is not that oil has stopped flowing. It is not that the technology to refine sufficient petroleum products for local consumption and export has been lost. Rather, the tragedy we face is that we have had a mainly prodigal leadership since military rule began sixty years ago. So, in our Egypt, we have sufficient oil reserves that will last at least the next sixty years. There was no fuel subsidy because we did not need to subsidise what we have. It is like asking a rich farmer with fertile soil and bursting barns of yam to subsidise the pounded yam his family will have for supper. What has happened is that a prodigal political class took over, deliberately ran down the refineries, refused to build new ones and, most criminally, insisted on denominating fuel in inflated dollar accounting. Their paper accounting is based on our country having no drop of oil, which we all know is false, and having to import finished products which are bought by dubious officials from their chosen partners, pay freight, insurance, port fees, demurrage and storage fees. These products are then handed over to a cartel which transports them through deliberately neglected or abandoned roads and sells them to hapless Nigerians at rates imposed by the cartel. In this dubious process is built what is touted as subsidy. Since the Babangida regime, this dubious subsidy mirage has been factored into our petroleum products. When the latest subsidy removal was touted on May 29, 2023, Nigerians were told the proceeds would be used for development. But what we have experienced is greater misery, multiplication of the hungry, dilapidating infrastructure, a rising number of out-of-school children, lack of mass housing, virtually abandoned basic healthcare and insecurity. Whenever we ask the administration what has been done with the so-called subsidy savings, it points at increasing the revenue allocation to states and local governments. It is aware that most leaders of these tiers are like cats being told to watch over fried fish. Deceptively, it does not point at itself as being the largest recipient of these extra funds, which remain unaccounted for. When President Tinubu announced that his administration had removed fuel subsidy, the price of a litre of PMS was increased from about N197 to an average N500. Today, it is thrice that price, and the government blames this insanity on the war in Iran. In this, the Tinubu government is behaving like the dirty widow with head lice creeping all over her hair who blames this on mourning her husband by not allowing a drop of water to touch her head since his demise. If the Nigerian government blames the war in Iran for the outrageous price of PMS in the country, why is Iran, which has suffered the catastrophe of having its leadership wiped out, children buried under the rubble of their classrooms, infrastructure and oil facilities bombed and punishing sanctions imposed by the United States, not been similarly affected? Honourable Victor Afam Oghene, Member, Federal House of Representatives, Ogbaru Constituency of Anambra State, debunked, with verifiable statistics, these childish fairy tales of the Tinubu government. He gave comparative statistics of PMS prices in four oil-producing countries: Iran, which has been at war for years; Libya, which has suffered state collapse since 2011 and had at least three factional governments in Tobruk, Tripoli and Benghazi; Saudi Arabia, which is engaged in war with neighbouring Yemen; and Nigeria, which is not at war. In his statistics, which the increasingly intolerant Tinubu government and its army of internet propagandists have not been able to fault, Honourable Oghene revealed that a litre of PMS in Iran is N38, Libya, N32, Saudi Arabia, N832, and Nigeria, at least N1,300. In contrast, the National Minimum Wage in Iran is N165,000, Libya is N210,000, Saudi Arabia, N1.4 million, and N70,000 in Nigeria! Oghene then analysed these basic statistics in value terms. He showed that the minimum wage in Iran can purchase 4,242 litres of PMS, Libya, 6,562 litres, Saudi Arabia, 1,700, and only 46 litres in Nigeria! Tragically, despite such sound analysis and the situation in the country, the Tinubu administration appears increasingly irritated, deaf to the cries of Nigerians and incapable of basic thinking. For instance, rather than examine the arguments of various patriots and pro-people activists on the issue of fuel subsidy and the calamitous effects on the populace, it is threatening Nigerians with dire consequences. In its unfathomable scare-mongering, the administration’s Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, threatened that even an inkling of the administration rethinking the subsidy issue would trigger capital flight. This, he claimed, would lead to the naira, which has already been devalued over fifty per cent by Tinubu, suffering a further sixty per cent devaluation. Oyedele told Nigerians this fable, not based on any analysis, but beliefs. He also claimed that this would raise the price of petrol to at least N2,000 per litre. Even as a product of Yale University and London School of Economics, and an advertised policy expert, the Honourable Minister could not provide the cost component of this his projected N2,000-per-litre PMS. We Nigerians never left our Egypt, so there is no issue of a return. It is the prodigals of the political class that need to return home, ask for forgiveness and stop suffocating the country. The post We never left Egypt, only prodigals need to return home, by Owei Lakemfa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Lula, la épica de la izquierda mundial
items.description: Difícil encontrar entre los 120 líderes mundiales que este septiembre tomaron la palabra en la sede de Naciones Unidas una trayectoria vital y política tan singular, y épica, como la del hijo de doña Lindu. La figura materna ocupa un lugar estelar en el relato que Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (80 años, Garanhuns, Pernambuco) ha construido sobre su vida. En su décimo discurso ante la Asamblea General, el presidente de Brasil (2003-2009 y desde 2023) habló de grandes conceptos, como soberanía, democracia o multilateralismo, pero en los mítines le encanta entrar en lo íntimo. Y contar que su madre le enseñó, con el ejemplo cotidiano, las lecciones que forjaron su carácter. “Doña Lindu, analfabeta, madre de ocho hijos pequeños, tuvo el valor de dejar a mi padre. Vivía en una choza, sacó adelante a ocho hijos y transformó a Lulinha en esta cosa bonita que hoy les habla”, recordó el veterano político al arrancar, en agosto, s u séptima campaña presidencial. El escenario era un guiño nostálgico al pasado, en ese estadio que arengaba a los obreros contra la dictadura. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Death toll in Nigeria village raided by gunmen rises to 48, police say
items.description: The death toll from Friday’s attack on a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba has risen to at least 48, police have told the BBC. The police had initially reported 10 deaths after unidentified gunmen on motorcycles raided the village of Binnari, looting shops and setting houses ablaze. More bodies were discovered on Sunday, according to state police spokesperson Victor Mshelizah, who said some of the victims had drowned while trying to escape the attackers, while others were killed in nearby bushes. Meanwhile, Amnesty International’s director for Nigeria said his organisation had confirmed 52 deaths, citing sources on the ground and members of the local community. The attack happened just after midday Muslim prayers, and the rampage went on for up to four hours. State police had initially recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call. The attackers had fled by the time officers arrived, but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, Taraba’s police told the BBC on Saturday. “We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen, though there were no casualties on their side or ours because the terrain is difficult and they’re used to the terrain,” Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said. Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told news agency AFP that the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece. “They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions,” he said. “They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack.” Isiyaku Musa, who survived the attack, told AFP: “People were running in different directions to escape the attack. Nobody knew where it was safe to go.” Amnesty’s Nigeria director Isa Sanusi has called for an impartial investigation into the killings, accusing the authorities of leaving rural communities “at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly committing atrocities with impunity”. Parts of north-eastern Nigeria have been affected by years of violence involving jihadist groups and armed gangs, which raid communities, abduct residents and demand ransoms. Similar armed groups operate in the country’s north-west and central regions. The latest attack comes as Nigeria prepares for elections next year, with insecurity expected to feature prominently in political debates. Survivors who spoke to AFP said they had counted at least 20 dead. “People were running in different directions to escape the attack,” Binnari resident Isiyaku Musa said. “Nobody knew where it was safe to go.” Another survivor, Sa’idu Nuhu, said that some people were still missing. Amnesty’s Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, told BBC News on Saturday that the NGO had spoken to some of the bereaved families who said up to 50 people had died. “The initial funeral had 37 people,” he said. Sanusi called for an impartial investigation into the killings, accusing the authorities of leaving rural communities “at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity”.

items.title: Houston’s message to Africa: Innovation must deliver more barrels, lower costs and better returns
items.description: By Kunle Odusola-Stevenson The future of Africa’s oil and gas industry will not be determined by the resources beneath its soil alone, but by how effectively it deploys technology, attracts investment and translates policy into commercial results. This was a central takeaway from the Society of Petroleum Engineers’ (SPE) Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition (ATCE) 2026, held in Houston, Texas, from October 21 to 23. Under the theme, “Exploring New Horizons with Innovative Solutions,” the conference brought together energy professionals to examine the technologies, engineering practices and operational strategies shaping the industry’s future. For Nigeria, where increasing production, developing natural gas resources and strengthening indigenous operators remain national priorities, the message was clear: innovation must translate into measurable business performance. The global energy industry is under pressure to deliver reliable supplies, improve capital efficiency and reduce environmental impacts. For Africa, these demands coincide with a pressing need to expand electricity access, industrialise economies and create productive employment. The challenge is not simply to defend the relevance of hydrocarbons, but to demonstrate that African energy resources can be developed competitively, responsibly and profitably. The lessons from Houston offer a practical starting point. Artificial intelligence, advanced reservoir analytics, predictive maintenance, drilling automation and digital production monitoring are creating opportunities to improve oil recovery, reduce equipment failures, shorten operational delays and strengthen investment decisions. Their significance lies not in technological novelty, but in their potential to improve the economics of producing assets. Consider Nigeria’s mature oilfields, many of which face declining production, ageing infrastructure, rising water cuts and expensive maintenance requirements. Better integration of geological data, well-performance records and production information can help operators identify underperforming wells, prioritise interventions and determine where additional investment is most likely to recover lost production. Predictive maintenance can similarly help operators identify early warning signs in pumps, compressors and other critical equipment before failures cause costly shutdowns. Improved drilling analytics can support better well planning, reduce non-productive time and strengthen operational safety. Meanwhile, methane monitoring and flare-management technologies can help operators identify emissions sources, reduce avoidable losses and improve environmental performance. These are practical applications for Nigeria’s oil and gas industry, not automatic outcomes of technology adoption. Results depend on reliable data, competent personnel, appropriate infrastructure and disciplined implementation. Every investment should therefore be assessed against measurable indicators, including incremental production, reduced downtime, lower operating costs, improved recovery and emissions reduction. This approach is particularly important as Nigeria’s upstream industry undergoes structural change. The transfer of selected onshore and shallow-water assets from international oil companies to indigenous operators has created opportunities for domestic companies to expand their participation and retain more value within the economy. Yet a change of ownership does not automatically produce higher output, stronger profitability or sustainable operations. Indigenous operators must combine ownership with the technical and financial capacity to manage complex reservoirs, rehabilitate infrastructure, improve recovery and meet environmental obligations. Access to technology, long-term financing, specialised engineering expertise and dependable evacuation systems will be critical to their success. Nigeria’s ambition to achieve three million barrels of crude oil production per day by 2030 must therefore be treated as an execution challenge rather than a statement of intent. New developments, improved recovery from existing fields, reduced production losses, reliable evacuation and sustained investment must work together to deliver the desired outcome. The leadership transition within the SPE Nigeria Council, from Engr. Francis Nwaochei to Engr. Etta Agbor, also presents an opportunity to strengthen the connection between global technical knowledge and local operating realities. Professional institutions such as SPE can support this process through applied research, technical training, industry collaboration and the development of Nigerian engineering talent capable of evaluating and deploying advanced technologies. However, technology alone cannot overcome an uncertain investment environment. Regulatory predictability remains fundamental. The Petroleum Industry Act provides an important statutory framework, but investors also require transparent fiscal arrangements, timely approvals, consistent regulatory decisions and clarity over contractual obligations. Effective regulation should protect public interests while enabling commercially viable projects to proceed without avoidable administrative delays. Security and infrastructure are equally important. Production cannot generate its full economic value if crude oil and gas cannot reach markets reliably. Pipeline disruptions, theft, infrastructure failures and insecurity increase operating costs, undermine revenues and weaken investor confidence. Government institutions, regulators, operators, security agencies and host communities must work together to protect infrastructure and strengthen the reliability of Nigeria’s energy supply chain. Environmental performance is also becoming integral to commercial competitiveness. Methane detection, flare reduction, emissions monitoring and environmental remediation increasingly influence investor assessments and access to international financing. Operators must incorporate these responsibilities into field-development plans and operating budgets rather than treating them as separate sustainability commitments. Beyond upstream production, Africa’s energy investment proposition extends across the value chain. Gas processing, pipelines, gas-to-power, domestic LNG and LPG distribution can support industrial growth where viable markets and bankable offtake arrangements exist. Refining and petrochemical development can create additional value through domestic processing, fertiliser production, manufacturing and associated logistics. Each opportunity, however, requires commercially realistic assumptions, dependable infrastructure and appropriate risk allocation. For international investors, the question is no longer simply whether Africa possesses substantial hydrocarbon resources. It is whether specific projects can offer credible returns, transparent governance, manageable risks and reliable access to markets. African governments and operators must make that case through predictable policies, technical competence and consistent delivery. Industry platforms such as the Nigeria International Energy Summit can help connect technology providers, indigenous operators, regulators, policymakers and international financiers. Their value should ultimately be measured by what follows the discussions: capital mobilised, partnerships established, technology deployed, infrastructure completed and production improved. The message from Houston to Abuja is unmistakable. Africa’s energy future will not be secured by resource abundance alone. It will depend on the disciplined convergence of engineering excellence, investment, reliable infrastructure, environmental responsibility and decisive policy execution. Nigeria has the resources and entrepreneurial potential to compete more effectively in the global energy economy. The task is to create the conditions that allow those advantages to translate into sustained production, industrial growth and shared prosperity. Africa must move beyond selling the promise of its resources to demonstrating the strength of its energy business case. Innovation must deliver more barrels, lower costs and better returns. That is how global technology can become local capability, investment can become productive capacity, and energy can become a foundation for lasting economic transformation. Odusola-Stevenson is CEO of The Legend & Legacy Company Ltd. items.title: Faîtière des caisses populaires du Burkina: le mérite au sein du réseau célébré
items.description: La Faîtière des caisses populaires du Burkina (FCPB) a organisé une soirée de reconnaissance et d’excellence de ses agents dénommé « BAORE », le vendredi 23 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. La Faîtière des caisses populaires du Burkina (FCPB) est soucieuse du travail bien fait au sein de ses institutions. Dans le but de célébrer les agents qui s’inscrivent dans cette dynamique de quête permanente de l’excellence, elle a organisé une soirée de reconnaissance à leur profit, dénommé « BAORE ». La cérémonie de distinction s’est déroulée, le vendredi 23 octobre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Durant cette soirée, au total 18 prix ont été décernés dans trois catégories. La première a récompensé des prix individuels aux travailleurs, notamment la meilleure caissière, le meilleur administrateur, le meilleur agent de crédit et secrétaire. La deuxième catégorie a concerné les cadres transversaux et la troisième a porté sur la gouvernance. Le représentant des récipien- daires, Salif Bruno Démé, a dédié son prix à son équipe et à ses proches, tout en exprimant sa joie et sa reconnaissance envers la FCPB. « C’est un prix qui vient m’interpeller à m’engager davantage », a-t-il confié. Le président du conseil d’administration de la FCPB, Augustin Sawadogo, a félicité la détermination de la direction générale de la faitière pour avoir ravivé les flammes des Prix BAORE. Pour lui, cet évènement est une occasion pour célébrer à la fois le mérite individuel, les performances collectives et une invite au renforcement collectif des capacités. « Notre ambition est d’en faire un levier de motivation, d’émulation positive et d’amélioration continue au service de nos membres et du développement économique et social de notre secteur », a-t-il souligné. Les BAORE sont un engagement collectif qui invite à apprécier le chemin parcouru et à se projeter avec détermination vers de nouveaux objectifs, a-t-il ajouté. « Dans un environnement marqué par des exigences croissantes en matière de qualité de service, de gouvernance, d’innovation et de performances, notre réseau doit poursuivre sa transformation tout en préservant des valeurs qui fondent son identité à savoir la solidarité, la proximité, la responsabilité et la confiance », a-t-il souligné. Il a, par la suite, souhaité que les distinctions reçues soient une source de fierté et une motivation supplémentaire pour franchir de nouvelles étapes. Le secrétaire général du ministère des Serviteurs du peuple, Suanyaba Rodrigue Oboulbiga, a salué cette initiative et a appelé toutes les organisations et entreprises, publiques comme privées, à emboiter les pas de la FCPB qui, selon lui, est en phase avec la vision de son ministère. Un appel à la rigueur et au travail bien fait « Être serviteur du peuple est avant tout un état d’esprit, une exigence civique et morale, et une manière d’exécuter son métier, d’assumer pleinement les responsabilités et de contribuer efficacement à la vie de la Nation. La directrice générale de la FCPB, Azaratou Sondo, a appelé les lauréats, ainsi que l’ensemble de ses collaborateurs à plus de rigueur et à servir d’exemple, aussi bien dans leurs caisses de base qu’au niveau de tout le Réseau des Caisses populaires du Burkina (RCPB). « C’est une lourde charge que chacun doit veiller à assumer au mieux, pour que les caisses populaires puissent toujours aller de l’avant et pouvoir réaliser leur mission, qui est de contribuer à l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations », a-t-elle rappelé. Mariama Claire MANDOMBA LOMPO Aissatou DIARRA (Stagiaire)
