But then along comes the scientific revolution. And yes, it is a natural response that people focus more intensely on these things. And as I said before, there seems to be this very common linkage between the matrix of belief and the frequency of these things happening. That’s a very solid, very rational argument, but it doesn’t explain everything. It just doesn’t. If in fact these things are happening and continued to happen, albeit with less frequency, you’re still dealing with a phenomenon. As I have discovered lately, there’s a word now being used to describe human beings who claim to have encountered nonhuman intelligence, and that word is experiencer . That’s also used for mystics. So in essence, a mystic telling you, “I understood the Trinity perfectly, but I can’t tell you” has the same trouble being believed as somebody who says, “This gray alien walked into my hotel room last night.” Brooks: There’s a famous episode which is sort of this clash. Rene Descartes, he’s early 17th century, he is actually a believer, but he decides he’s gonna sweep away all this tradition and knowledge that’s built up, and he’s gonna start from scratch. He’s gonna use pure reason, just logical, follow one step after another, and he makes sure he’s shielded from emotion. God forbid he should love somebody. And he’s trying to build up the whole edifice of human knowledge. And at exactly the same time, this other guy in France, Blaise Pascal, takes a look at what Descartes is doing and immediately hates him. Blaise Pascal is no random humanist. He was one of the greatest mathematicians to ever live. He was a technologist. He built a sort of early calculating machine. He was a scientist. He studied vacuums. So he had scientific rigor on his side, and he was saying, “I’m not against Descartes’s reason, but I have many other forms of knowledge that I use to understand the world.” The “spirit of genius” and the “spirit of finesse,” I think he called it. And he famously said, “The heart has reasons that reason knows not of.” And so he’s saying to Descartes, “You’re taking away other ways of knowing . ” And I think the clinching argument—it’s so amazing he understood this right away. We’re at this civilizational fork in the road. He says the problem with rationalism is not its admiration for reason, but its failure to recognize any other kind of knowledge. He’s saying, “You’re amputating me.” He’s talking out of his own experience of how he has studied the world. Eire: Plus he had a mystical experience. Brooks: Famously at the Night of Fire. Eire: Sewn into the lining of his coat: God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers. This distinction being made between these two forms of cognition. I’m so glad you brought up Pascal because he’s a contemporary. But there’s so many. When you’re dealing with the past—again, a different country—you find anomalous synchronicities all the time. One of the witnesses to St. Joseph of Cupertino’s levitations was a Saxon prince, Johann Friedrich of Saxony. And not just any Saxony, the Saxony that Luther had been part of. For some reason, he’s in Italy, and nobody has figured out what he was doing there. But he sees Joseph of Cupertino up in the air and he converts to Catholicism. Johann Friedrich. Oh my God. This is the same man who hired Leibniz as his librarian. Did he and Leibniz ever meet in the hallway, so to speak? And to talk about these things? A little thought experiment that I engage in my book: Yes, Newton and Joseph Cupertino walked the Earth, the same time. What if Newton had taken time off and done the grand tour and run into Joseph Cupertino? They could have. Yes, but they didn’t. They just didn’t. And Newton spent much of his later life trying to figure out the law of prophecy. Brooks: So we’re talking about this crucial time in Western history at least, where science is moving, and faith is moving in a different way. It seems to me you could look over periods of scientific advance—faith rises to respond. And so the period I know best is the late 19th century, the Industrial Revolution. You’ve got these machines. In the late 19th century, Henry Adams, who was in the same family as John Quincy Adams and John Adams, he goes to a bunch of world fairs. And he sees what they were obsessed with in the Chicago World’s Fair. He writes a chapter in his book, which is more famous than the rest of—well, the book’s pretty famous too, called The Education of Henry Adams —but the chapter is called “The Dynamo and the Virgin.” The Virgin, he says—different eras in time have different power sources. And in the 13th century, the Virgin was a tremendous power source in Europe, and we get all these cathedrals that they were wanting to buy ’cause the Virgin was their power source. And he says, “That’s going away.” And he writes in that chapter—humans have a tendency to worship power sources, and people are gonna start worshiping machines. It’s not clear what he thinks about it, but at the exact same moment, there are a lot of other people, or roughly in that industrial period, who really mined it. And then the part I hadn’t clued in until reading your book, ’cause you mentioned this, at exactly this moment, late 19th century, a lot of the world goes gaga over seances. People you wouldn’t expect, like Arthur Conan Doyle, the founder of Sherlock Holmes, Mr. Rational. You mention Abraham Lincoln’s wife. A lot of serious people were sitting around doing seances and Ouija boards and stuff like that. Eire: And that’s kind of the tip of the iceberg because this is the same period that gives us the Latter-day Saints, the Millerites, and eventually the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Theosophy, which becomes immensely popular. Brooks: Explain what that is. Eire: Theosophy is a blend of Western occult mysticism with basically Hinduism and Buddhism. And it was enormously popular, here in the United States, but also throughout the world. The American Theosophical Society, which for a while was based in Philadelphia, sent missionaries all around the world. I learned this from a dissertation I read back when I was at the University of Virginia. Otherwise, I would not have found this fact, which I find fascinating: The two most successful missions that the American Theosophical Society had were Brazil and Cuba. But they’re also immensely popular throughout Europe. Anyway, the list could be longer of all these other things. Arthur Conan Doyle came here to New Haven during his American tour and spoke at Woolsey Hall. Brooks: Which is the big hall here on campus. Eire: Yes. The big auditorium. On spirit photography. And it was packed. Standing room only. This spiritualism only intensifies during and right after the First World War. Brooks: That makes sense because there’s so many dead people. Eire: Especially all the dead young people, and parents desperate to come to terms with this. The Society for Psychic Studies is established in London in the late 19th century. There’s such a long list of other things that emerge at this very same time, occultism and everything else. This is because, as I see it—Pascal’s complaint, which is personal, can have a social and cultural dimension to it. When you take away belief in something that has ultimate meaning in another dimension other than this—because everybody’s body will give out on them and they will die, right? When you take that away—for lack of a better term, and I hate this term, disenchantment —you disenchant the world, the world will try to re-enchant itself. And it always does so, or often does so in very weird ways. Sometimes in very, very bad ways. The French Revolution. The Bolshevik Revolution. The Third Reich. If you look at those three, they are aggressive attempts to re-enchant the world differently. They have religious symbols. They have feasts. They have holidays. They have rituals. You name it, but the ultimate thing is the revolution. Brooks: The Marxist revolutions also laid claim to science too,though they were clearly secular religions. Eire: But they still have the trappings of a religion and require belief in an orthodoxy. And in some kind of apocalyptic future, right? Brooks: This brings me to today. So we’re in the world of AI now, and tech, and Elon Musk, and if you go to the Silicon Valley, they also have a kind of religion. They worship a god, which is intelligence. They believe in sin, which is inefficiency. They believe in moral progress, which is optimization. They believe in eternal life, which is transhumanism. You can download your brain on a computer and live forever. And so they’ve got it all going on, even though they would deny that they are religious, but it looks very much like a religion serving assertive existential longings. Eire: And given human instinct, that seems to be part of human history, that whenever something or someone comes along that seems to have immense power, or a combination of immense intelligence and immense power, people will venerate this. That’s one of the threats of AI that doesn’t get much attention, but what I think is a real possibility is that if, in fact, we get artificial intelligence, which by the way, can also be called nonhuman intelligence—if we got one that’s super intelligent enough, of course you’re going to have people who will not only use it, but have their whole lives directed by it. Brooks: You mentioned something that stuck in my head from a few minutes ago: that you don’t like the word disenchantment . Why is that? Eire: It’s sprinkled with fairy dust. The word in English enchantment has too much of an emotional baggage attached to it. It’s got an emotional dimension to it. But what happens when you take religion away is not disenchantment, not in that sense. It’s something much more aggressive. And what you lose is not emotion. What you lose is precisely, as Pascal complained, this other dimension. So that’s why I don’t like it. And especially too, I have personal reasons to complain because the subject I’ve been working on throughout my entire career falls into the category of disenchantment of the world. But all the definitions of enchantment or disenchantment that have been thrown at me—some of them ridiculous. For instance, may he rest in peace, Robert Scribner, a historian of the same time period, who said, “Protestants really didn’t disenchant the world, because they still had rituals.” I said, “What do you mean? Is that your sole criterion for enchantment or disenchantment? Of course people are going to have rituals. Government have rituals, right?” So it’s a very weak word. I wish there were a better word that people agreed on. This fuzzy word started to be used in 1930, when Talcott Parsons translated Max Weber and his phrase “Entzauberung der Welt,” with the word zauber right in the middle, which means “magic” in German. And he was very clear throughout several of his texts—he meant magic. Brooks: So you mentioned Max Weber. He wrote this process of rationalization, which led, I think in one translation, to what we call the “iron cage,” which is where we humans are stuck in this iron cage. And as a result, people’s spiritual lives shrivel, and in his words they become, I think it was, “specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart.” And I think that’s real. I live in Washington. I’m surrounded by specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart. Eire: His word for that was Entzauberung , not disenchantment. Brooks: Okay. And what, how would you translate that? Eire: Zauber is “magic.” Brooks: I see. Eire: Right? Which he also said in one sentence, that Entzauberung means taking away magie , M-A-G-I-E, which was the learned German word for magic . What he meant was that there’s no transcendent other dimension. And he also spoke of prophets. The only way that the world can be enchanted again is through prophets. And by prophets, he meant something like mystics, who actually have a real existential connection to something larger that can then convince other people that there’s more to life than this table and this microphone. He also spoke of the choices that people are left in this—let’s stay with disenchantment—disenchanted world. The choices that people are left with, it’s basically kind of a polytheism. Where you have to choose between different gods. It goes back to this insight that is a constant throughout the Christian tradition, this realization that human beings have an innate need for meaning. And that meaning has to be ultimate, not just proximate. It has to be ultimate. So we do our damnedest to make it up. Or as Pascal said, we do our damnedest to keep ourselves distracted so that we don’t look at the abyss that lies just a few feet away. Brooks: I think that distraction’s a key point. You can go through life not thinking about this stuff. There are two things that seem to be going on. I have a friend and former New York Times colleague, Ross Douthat, who argued that as society secularizes, you don’t get atheism; you get the strangest religions you can think of. There’s a book by a woman named Tara Isabella Burton called Strange Rites , where she details all these new religions that are popping up as people try to find some meaning somewhere. And this reminds me, I hadn’t made the connection to that 19th-century upstate New York— Eire: The burned-over district. Brooks: —when all these new religions were popping up all over the place. But then I think there’s other things going on, which is there really is a dis—well, I don’t wanna use that word; you’ll reach across the table and punch me—but there is a materialistic mentality that is definitely more prevalent today than in the 17th century. And I think that’s sad. So I guess my question for you is: When you’re writing all this stuff, are you partly motivated by a disquiet with the present? Eire: Oh, definitely. Most definitely. Yes. I’m very disquieted, and I’ve been disquieted for quite some time, since childhood. But my present baggage, let’s put it that way, has to do with the way in which one can be so easily silenced or ridiculed for merely suggesting that something else should be taken seriously. That’s enough to put you in the category of an alien abductee. David Brooks: The book came out, I think, in ’23. How has the reaction response been, both from the professional historical community and from the wider public? Eire: Well, the professional historical community is so slow. Our book reviews sometimes take two to three years. So I have yet to see very many reviews in professional journals. But in other venues, the response has been overwhelmingly positive. There’ve been a couple of nasty book reviews. I expected them. One of them with a beautiful sentence: “This is a deeply unserious book.” Brooks: That’s a compliment where I come from. Eire: Another reviewer found it necessary, for whatever reason, to bring up the fact that I was Cuban, and therefore I’m credulous and very fond of magical realism. Brooks: You’re Gabriel García Márquez. Eire: Yes, I am, like all Latin Americans. Yeah. You know, we’re all a little ... Brooks: That’s why we love you. Now I have two final topics. One is, and I wanted to ask you about this—you say there’s a supernatural mentality and there’s a material mentality. But you introduce this concept that there’s also a third way of believing in the middle there, which you say is a “vast polymorphous, variegated middle between these two extreme poles, abounding in myriad attitudes and convictions.” As a natural temperamental moderate, that sounds good to me. Eire: And I think that’s basically my position. When you’re faced with unknowns, what do you do? How do you make up your mind? I just thought of this, and your question prompted this to appear—I take the same attitude to quantum entanglement and the Big Bang that I do to these phenomena. Until I see somebody up in the air and say, “Yes, I’m seeing this,” I can’t say I’ve experienced it, in the same way that you can say about any kind of religious experience, “Yes, I have experienced this.” I’ve been to many religious services where I have been so transported, I guess is a good way to put it. I’m not there in the room. I mean, I know I’m there, but I’m not there. And some of them have been very odd moments too. In houses of worship other than Catholic. It’s happened. That’s one thing. But seeing somebody up in the air, though. But quantum entanglement, what do you do with this? And what do you do with the latest images from the Webb telescope telling us that the Big Bang may be something else? Brooks: The scientists who I know, whom I admire, some of them are just arrogantly dismissive of all spiritual experience. I say, “Well, you explain how consciousness emerged from the brain, then I’ll take your arrogance as somewhat earned. Or you explain what happened before the Big Bang. You can’t do that. You explain quantum entanglement.” You can’t explain any of this stuff. The existence of the universe and consciousness, which is our primary ways to understand the world, if you can’t explain these two things—these are the two biggest things in our world. Eire: If I were younger, I think this is the area I would dive into next. All this work that’s being done on mind and consciousness, which is, in fact, a connecting point, a nexus, very natural nexus, religion and science. But I have so much reading to do. Can’t do it now. Brooks: So many years have been wasted trying to solve the consciousness problem. Okay, the final question. All of our conversation has been leading up to one question: Did they fly? Eire: Yes. And I don’t mean to put any qualifiers on this. I’m willing to take that testimony as one would in a court of law, although there’s no physical evidence. That’s the one difference. There’s no murder weapon, let’s say. But let me put it this way: I think it’s highly, highly likely, especially since we have reports. What I find very annoying, though, extremely annoying, is that cameras and film have been in existence for well over a century. Brooks: That’s the obvious rejoinder to your belief. What’s your answer? Eire: Right. Where is it? Where is it? Some television show tried to trick me, said, “We have film of somebody levitating. Would you watch it?” They were doing this live. And, yeah, it was obvious this person was spinning on a highwire. I said, “Well, you’re not showing what’s at the other end here. Is there another tree or another pole?” They said, “Yeah, we didn’t wanna tell you ahead of time. We just wanted your reaction.” Brooks: I must say, I still am not quite there where you are, but I’m struck by how much in our popular culture, how much flying there is. Superman is flying. Harry Potter is flying on his broom. There’s a lot of flying. Look, we accept this so easily when we think it’s a superhero story or fiction. Eire: Well, we have maglev trains. It’s not like this is physically impossible. You can actually physically levitate small frogs with sound waves. Brooks: Oh really? Eire: Yes, that’s been done. Brooks: It’s very unpleasant for the frogs. Eire: Well, coins—everybody has seen coins levitate. But you can take a little tiny frog, and with acoustic, levitation can take place. So it’s not physiologically or physically impossible. One of my early talks on the subject long, long before the book came out, there was a doctor in the audience. I always love the first question because it’s always the most troublesome: Did these people have a lot of iron in their diets, by the way? Maybe they were magnets in the room. Brooks: That’s a lot of iron. Eire: I said, “No, I don’t think so.” Yeah. I don’t think so. Brooks: Carlos, I really appreciate your taking the time, and I really enjoyed our conversation. Eire: Oh, my pleasure. Brooks: I’m hoping that people come away with their mind expanded, but also come away with—when in life we encounter people whose political views, religious views, whatever views seem crazy to us, we pause and we say, “Where are you coming from? Let me try to see the world from your eyes.” And that strikes me as the essence of democracy. Eire: It is, and it’s essential for survival. Brooks: I thought one of the most interesting moments in my conversation with Carlos is when I asked him right at the end, “Did they fly?” And he flat out said, “Yes, they did.” Think of the intellectual courage it takes to say that. A lot of people are going to think that’s ridiculous, but he’s a man of his convictions. He thinks supernatural realities are real. He’s also a man who’s done the work. He spent the years in the archives reading all these testimonies, so he’s got some substance behind what he’s thinking. I personally am not quite convinced. I think if human beings had the capacity to levitate, then we’d find one video of it, or somebody would be doing it today. But I believe that the people who described their levitation sincerely believed they were flying, just the way I might sincerely believe I’m driving down the New Jersey Turnpike. And how did they believe this? I don’t know. But I respect the fact that they did it. When it comes to humans, variability is the rule. We’ve got a lot of different mindsets out there, and people hold sincere beliefs that seem bonkers to the rest of us, but are probably worthy of our respect. Thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Carlos Eire. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic , in partnership with Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . See you next week.

items.title: Conakry : le ministre Bourouno lance la 3è phase du concours d’accès à l’ENA de Guinée
items.description: L’École nationale d’administration (ENA) de Guinée a franchi une nouvelle étape dans le processus de recrutement des élèves de sa toute première promotion. Ce dimanche, 570 candidats, présélectionnés à l’issue des épreuves de questionnaires à choix multiples (QCM), ont pris part à la troisième phase du concours, organisée à l’Université Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry. À l’issue de cette étape, 240 candidats seront retenus pour poursuivre leur parcours au sein de cette institution appelée à contribuer à la transformation de l’administration publique guinéenne. Présent sur le site pour lancer les épreuves, le ministre de la Modernisation de l’Administration et de la Fonction publique, Faya François Bourouno, a insisté sur la rigueur du processus de sélection, le respect de l’égalité des chances et la recherche du mérite. Pour le gouvernement, la mise en place de cette école constitue un levier de formation de cadres capables de répondre aux exigences d’une administration publique plus performante et davantage tournée vers les citoyens. « Nous sommes en train de recruter les élèves de la première promotion du diplôme de l’École nationale d’administration (ENA). Conformément au protocole qui encadre les programmes de formation, nous accordons une grande rigueur au processus d’élaboration des programmes, notamment à celui de la sélection des participants au programme du diplôme », a expliqué le ministre. Selon le ministre Bourouno, le concours repose sur un processus de sélection structuré en quatre étapes. Après l’examen des dossiers de candidature et les épreuves de QCM organisées il y a quelques semaines, les candidats admissibles ont été convoqués ce dimanche pour les épreuves écrites. Une quatrième étape est prévue dans le dispositif de sélection. Cette troisième phase vise notamment à évaluer les capacités rédactionnelles des candidats, en complément de leurs aptitudes à répondre aux questions à choix multiples. Un critère que le ministre juge essentiel pour les futurs élèves fonctionnaires appelés à intégrer l’administration publique. « Il y a la capacité à répondre aux questions sous forme de QCM, mais nous voulons également tester et évaluer les capacités rédactionnelles des futurs élèves fonctionnaires de l’École nationale d’administration », a-t-il précisé. Au-delà des connaissances théoriques, les autorités entendent ainsi s’assurer que les futurs élèves disposent des aptitudes nécessaires pour suivre une formation exigeante et, à terme, exercer des responsabilités au sein des services publics. Le mérite et l’égalité des chances au cœur du recrutement Lors de sa visite, le ministre a également vérifié les conditions matérielles et organisationnelles mises en place pour le bon déroulement des épreuves. Il s’est dit satisfait du dispositif observé dans les salles d’examen, estimant que les dispositions prises permettaient aux candidats de composer dans des conditions appropriées. « Nous sommes à la recherche du mérite, à travers le processus de sélection. Nous savons également que l’école reposera sur l’excellence et la rigueur dans tout le processus d’enseignement », a-t-il déclaré. Pour garantir le bon déroulement de cette phase, plusieurs mesures administratives, logistiques, sécuritaires et communicationnelles ont été mobilisées. Elles portent notamment sur la constitution des dossiers, l’information des candidats, la mise à disposition des salles et la sécurisation du centre d’examen. À cette occasion, François Bourouno a salué l’appui du rectorat de l’Université Gamal Abdel Nasser de Conakry, ainsi que celui du ministère de l’Enseignement supérieur et de la Recherche scientifique, pour la mise à disposition du cadre ayant accueilli les candidats. Une école au service de la qualité de l’administration publique Si l’accès au diplôme de l’ENA est soumis à une sélection rigoureuse, le ministre a tenu à rappeler que l’établissement a vocation à proposer des programmes diversifiés et à rester ouvert à différents profils. Il a toutefois souligné que le programme diplômant destiné à former les futurs cadres de l’administration nécessite un niveau d’exigence particulier. « L’école est ouverte à tout le monde. C’est pourquoi nous avons diversifié les programmes. Cependant, le programme conduisant au diplôme de l’ENA doit être mis en œuvre avec toute la rigueur nécessaire », a-t-il indiqué. À travers ce recrutement, les autorités ambitionnent de constituer une première promotion répondant aux exigences de formation, de compétence et de professionnalisme attendues dans la fonction publique. L’objectif final, selon le ministre, est d’améliorer la qualité des prestations administratives et de faciliter l’accès des citoyens aux services publics. « La finalité recherchée est de faire en sorte que le service public offert aux citoyens soit un service de qualité et accessible à tous », a conclu le ministre. La sélection des 240 futurs élèves constituera ainsi une étape déterminante dans le lancement des activités de formation de l’ENA. Au-delà du concours, l’enjeu est de préparer des cadres capables de contribuer à la modernisation de l’État et à l’amélioration durable du fonctionnement de l’administration guinéenne. Youssouf Keita L’article Conakry : le ministre Bourouno lance la 3è phase du concours d’accès à l’ENA de Guinée est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Israël : des milliers de manifestants contre Netanyahou à trois jours des législatives
items.description: Des milliers d'Israeliens ont defile le 24 octobre a Tel Aviv contre le gouvernement du Premier ministre Benjamin Netanyahou, a trois jours d'elections legislatives qui s'annoncent serrees. La manifestation, organisee par le Conseil d'Octobre, un collectif de familles de victimes et d'otages de l'attaque du 7 octobre 2023, visait notamment a reclamer des comptes sur les defaillances securitaires qui ont permis cette attaque du Hamas, la plus meurtriere de l'histoire d'Israel. Les manifestants se sont rassembles sur la place des Otages, devenue depuis le debut de la guerre a Gaza un lieu emblematique des mobilisations en faveur du retour des personnes enlevees lors de l'attaque. Le Conseil d'Octobre demande la mise en place d'une commission d'enquete independante, une initiative jusqu'ici refusee par le gouvernement Netanyahou. Les principales figures de l'opposition avaient annonce leur participation au rassemblement. Parmi elles figuraient le centriste Gadi Eisenkot, le chef de l'opposition Yaïr Lapid, son allie Naftali Bennett, l'ancien ministre de la Defense Avigdor Liberman et le dirigeant du parti Les Democrates, Yaïr Golan. Ces responsables se sont engages a creer une commission d'enquete en cas de victoire electorale. Des elections sous haute tension Le scrutin du 27 octobre, le premier depuis l'attaque du 7 octobre 2023, est largement presente comme un test politique pour Benjamin Netanyahou, au pouvoir depuis 2022. Selon les derniers sondages autorises a etre publies la veille, le bloc du Premier ministre etait credite de 50 sieges, contre 52 pour le bloc d'opposition constitue autour de Gadi Eisenkot. Ces projections restaient eloignees des 61 sieges necessaires pour obtenir une majorite a la Knesset. Au-dela des defaillances securitaires, la campagne electorale est marquee par les consequences de la guerre a Gaza, les tensions regionales et les critiques internationales visant la politique israelienne, notamment en Cisjordanie occupee. Certains electeurs de l'opposition esperent qu'une alternance permettra d'ameliorer les relations d'Israel avec la communaute internationale. Benjamin Netanyahou a egalement suscite des reactions apres avoir evoque le 23 octobre la preparation d'un plan visant a developper une economie alternative pour contourner d'eventuelles sanctions internationales, notamment dans le secteur bancaire. Il a cite la blockchain parmi les pistes envisagees. Gadi Eisenkot a tourne cette proposition en derision sur les reseaux sociaux, estimant qu'un tel projet risquerait d'isoler davantage Israel de l'economie mondiale.

items.title: 'Not a single tree' will be cut down to upgrade Islamabad's F-9 Park, interior minister assures residents
items.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday assured the residents of Islamabad that “not a single tree” will be cut down during the planned upgradation of the city’s F-9 Park. In a post on X, the minister shared an Instagram video of an Islamabad resident requesting that if the park were to be developed, more greenery be planted instead of concrete buildings. In his response, Naqvi recognised that F-9 Park — also known as Fatima Jinnah Park — “holds a special place in the hearts” of Islamabad residents and clarified that no trees would be removed in the process of developing the park. “Let me make it absolutely clear that not a single tree will be cut, 100 per cent guaranteed,” he said. He further vowed that there would be “no new concrete structures”. Instead, the planned upgrades included “better lighting, a beautiful lake, coffee shops, improved walkways” and the plantation of “thousands” of more trees in the park, the interior minister added. “Our only goal is to make F-9 Park greener, safer, more beautiful, and more enjoyable for families and visitors,” he said. Naqvi has previously shared plans to upgrade and improve recreational facilities around Islamabad, working with the Capital Development Authority (CDA) to create a “more developed, clean, green, beautiful, safe, environmentally sustainable and citizen-friendly capital” while enhancing its tourism potential. In April, he sought a comprehensive plan for transforming F-9 Park on the model of London’s Hyde Park, and for developing recreational facilities near Shahdara Dam. However, development projects in the historically green city have not always been favourably received by residents, inciting concerns particularly over deforestation and clearance of land for residential areas. At the start of this year, a large-scale tree removal drive took place in at least three locations in the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT), including around the Shakarparian area, sparking widespread public criticism. The CDA maintained that only paper mulberry trees were removed as they had been causing pollen allergies , and Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry assured lawmakers that a greater number of trees would be planted in the coming months. In 2024, the Supreme Court (SC) took notice of the removal of trees in F-9 Park and restrained the CDA from cutting trees in the area. The CDA, in response, told the SC that about 7,000 paper mulberry trees had been cut down because they caused allergies.

items.title: Ça médit sur TikTok (le billet d’Omar DIOUF)
items.description: Diodio Glow Skin, Rox (encore elle), Adamo, Kaliphone… Une nouvelle affaire dakaroise sur TikTok. À la longue, on croirait que ce réseau social chinois est créé pour les potins sénégalais. En tout cas, c’est comme si. On y calomnie, insulte, règle des comptes à longueur d’heures, de journées, de mois… Certaines loueraient même les services d’énergumènes pour se charger du sale boulot, faire mal virtuellement à ses adversaires ou ennemies. Il y a trois jours, la dame Nogaye Kara écopait d’une amende financière pour discours contraire aux bonnes mœurs. Lors d’un live, elle se crêpait le chignon avec une certaine Mimi. À la longue, on se perd dans ce mélodrame à la Sénégalaise dans TikTok. À défaut de faire bon usage des technologies, certains de nos compatriotes en abusent en radotage de mensonges, en diffamation et autres commérages. La Division spéciale de cybersécurité et les procureurs ont vraiment du pain sur la planche… omar.diouf@lesoleil.sn

items.title: Naufrage du Prospector 5 : Oligui Nguema promet de rendre publiques les conclusions de l’enquête
items.description: Mobiliser tous les moyens de l’État, informer les familles en priorité et faire la lumière sur le sinistre. Après le naufrage du Prospector 5 au large de Mayumba, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema annonce avoir donné des instructions au gouvernement. Il exige également une coopération totale de BW Energy, alors que cinq travailleurs restent portés disparus. « Les Gabonais ont le droit de savoir ce qui s’est passé » : Oligui Nguema face à l’exigence de vérité après le naufrage du Prospector 5. © D.R. «Les Gabonais ont le droit de savoir ce qui s’est passé.» Dans un message publié sur sa page Facebook, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema s’engage sur la transparence de l’enquête concernant le naufrage de la plateforme de forage Prospector 5, survenu samedi 24 octobre au large de Mayumba. Le chef de l’État affirme que les investigations établiront les causes et les responsabilités et que «ses conclusions seront rendues publiques» . Tous les moyens de l’État mobilisés Le président dit suivre «heure par heure» les opérations de recherche et de sauvetage des cinq travailleurs portés disparus. Il annonce avoir demandé au gouvernement de mobiliser tous les moyens de l’État, en premier lieu la Marine nationale, afin que les recherches se poursuivent « sans relâche » et que les familles soient informées en priorité. Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema indique également s’être entretenu avec le directeur général de BW Energy. Selon son récit, celui-ci lui a assuré que les équipes de l’entreprise interviennent avec Borr Drilling et les autorités gabonaises pour retrouver les disparus. «Je lui ai rappelé que l’État attend de l’opérateur une coopération totale, sur les recherches comme sur l’enquête» , souligne le chef de l’État. Une exigence de sécurité pour les travailleurs en mer Le président adresse ses pensées aux disparus et à leurs proches, tout en saluant les 110 personnes sauvées et le courage des secours intervenus dans la nuit. Il exprime aux familles «la solidarité entière de la Nation» . Au-delà de l’urgence, il affirme vouloir porter une exigence de sécurité auprès de chaque opérateur présent dans les eaux gabonaises : «Ceux qui travaillent en mer pour notre pays doivent pouvoir le faire en sécurité.» L’article Naufrage du Prospector 5 : Oligui Nguema promet de rendre publiques les conclusions de l’enquête est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

Jameh Mosque of Fahraj: A timeless architectural treasure near Yazd
items.description: TEHRAN - Located near the historic city of Yazd in central Iran, the Jameh Mosque of Fahraj, also known as Masjid-i Jami of Fahraj, is a remarkable destination for travelers interested in history, architecture and Iran’s Islamic heritage. Distinguished by its simple earthen construction, ancient vaults and historic minaret, the mosque offers a glimpse into an important period in the evolution of Iranian religious architecture.
